SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with
Chuck Green
Tapes 1, 2 and 3

Washington, D. C.
August 1977

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PMcC
PROCEEDINGS

This is Chuck Green, reel number one, interview. I guess the first question I have for you, Chuck, is this. What first excited you to dance? As a child, what was the first thing that really turned you on?
My mother.
Okay. Tell me a little bit more about that.

Well, she used to go to a town called Thomasville, Georgia. That's a little ways from Fitzgerald, Georgia, my birthplace, and she'd taken dancing lessons for just to keep her-- health purposes. You know, that's the she wanted to be trim. It was like an exercise with her, you know. And I was a little one at the time. And she used to take me along, you see. And --
How old were you then?

I was about three years old at that time. I'd say I was just a little one, (inaudible), you know, little baby. See, rather than to leave me home, you see, she taken me along, because I was an only child. And I used to watch her during her class with the dancing teacher, you see. Very good, lady was.
I wished I remembered my mother's dancing teacher's name, because she was a lovely lady. Well, I enjoyed it, you know, but I really wasn't strong enough to do anything.

I mean like --
(Laughter)
-- bodily, you see. But I fell in love with the dancing,
the activity of the body, you see. And she used to be
talking sometimes, she'd have me, after we'd get back home,
she'd be talking about herself and her teacher, you know.
I wonder why she taught me that, why she had me do this and
why she had me to do that, different steps and things. It
was kind of -- says, kind of into ballet. See, her teacher
was a ballet dancer, sometime or other, but she was known as
a dancing teacher, you see, and my mother used to -- I think
it was the horn.

I think it was called the horn, Harris J. or some-
thing, you know. And she would be talking about my father,
say she was going to surprise him. I got a surprise for Sam
today, you know. Once when he come home, I'm going to --
he'll be asking me about what I learned or something, you
see. I'll have a surprise for him, you see.

So in the meantime I'm a hearer. I'm a listener.
I'm hearing my mother comment to herself about activities,
you see. Now, as the time goes on, my father would come home
and, sure enough, he would do exactly what she'd say, you
know. Well, what did you do today? What happened? How was
the -- how was Thomasville, you know? Was the dancing
teacher there? And my mother would say, 'Oh, yes, said, she's

making a new person out of me, you know, says, you know what I learned today? No. She said, I had the baby with me, you know, because he wouldn't understand. He wouldn't know. You know, hee-hee, you know. Well, I knew. I could see, and I could understand, sight sure enough (inaudible) right?
So soon after she would do this horn, see? I think it's from the Irish jig or the -- what this -- some -- Could be the (Inaudible) was very popular.
Yeah, that's it, dee-dee-duh-duh-duh-duh-duh.
Jigs --
She could really do this, you know, and I mean -- Folk dancing --
(Inaudible) Johnson
-- I enjoyed it, you know, because it really was a pretty thing. So --
That's basically what it was, the sailor's dance?

Yeah, that's what it was. What my father said it was. He'd say, Well, what are you doing that for? Do you know that sailors, they're the worst talkers, you know, because sailors are known to use vulgarity, you know, profanity, you know. He'd run down there, and she ran back and laughed, you see. So I knew he was going to say that. So (inaudible), you know, say that.
(Laughter)
What was the dance? What exactly was it?
Huh?
What exactly was the dance? How would you describe it? What -- the dance that you were seeing --
Well, it really was the authentic dance itself because that's what the teacher taught her.
Was it mostly footwork or --
Yes, foot and body, that's --

Yes, it's a folk dance, you know, heel-toe, heel-toe kind of thing, you see. Anybody that was familiar with clog dancing, that's what it's all about, anybody's familiar with old Irish folk dancing or anything in that category, they're very familiar with the heel-toe. And you find a lot of heel and toe in tap dancing. Bo Jangles -- Bill Robinson --
Yes, his dancing is based on that.
So continue.

Well, as I say, I cannot say years because only two years came, and then we had to leave Fitzgerald, Georgia. My parents didn't actually separate or divorce or anything, but they separated because my father had one of his brother's daughters there that he had been taking

care of because her parents got killed, murdered, you know, covered wagon some time ago. And she was left in his care. So he was -- he had to take her. Her name was Annie B. -- Annie B., you see, take her to Leslie, Georgia, I think it is. And my mother and I, he sent us to -- my mother -- my mother's mother's city where she was in, Atlanta, Georgia. So we went our ways, you know.
And that's when most of my music lessons discontinued, see. At that time I was being taught like -- I had a little violin I used to play a little bit.
How old were you then?

I was about five, about five years old, you see. And -- so we went to Atlanta, Georgia, and my mother's mother, you see. And I was entered into another school, public school, Davis T. Howard, you see. And they had a procedure in that grade, first grade, which is called kindergarten, right? Like when you get up to the head of the class, it would be about eight of us in the head of the class, whenever you get there, but you would get to the head of the class by doing some kind of compositioning.

And they used to have people come there observing the head of the class, and one time they had some people from radio, 'Children's Hour'; they came there. And each one of us in the head of the class would have to get up and read something from our composition.

So, that time, I was into singing, like -- so I read something from my composition, and they wanted to know if I sang or did anything, what did I do besides -- they liked my voice or something, body. So I told them that I had been taking singing lessons, you know. And -- all right -- so they --
Now, you were taking singing lessons --
Yeah.
-- along with your mother when she went to her classes?

No, no, that was after we came -- left Fitzgerald, Georgia. See, this was in Atlanta, Georgia, which was a city. It was called the Little New York City, I mean at that time, but it was still Atlanta. And so they asked me what kind of singing did I do. So I -- luckily I could say that I sang like some famous people at that time, like Mort Downey. He was very famous. And another I did, like a little Paul Robeson, you know, but as a child, you see, I could do bass voice like a little bit. And it's kind of, you know, that's what they wanted, and they needed that kind of thing.

So I told them I sang like Kate Smith, you know, and this 'When the Moon Comes Over the Mountain' and so on. So anyhow I was chosen for the 'Children's Hour', right? So now, once the -- that's the American Broadcasting Company.

Once they chose, you see, they would continue your education, but you would get more. You could go to dancing school. You could go to -- you know, learn a lot of different things that you wouldn't ordinarily learn in the first grade of a school, see.

So it went on pretty good for a while, about a week and a half. So -- until this announcer came one day -- he said, as -- he said that the royal family was coming there with their children, see, because in a radio station there you never have any audience. It's just the microphone and the performers, you see. So they -- being the royal family, naturally they come up into the studio and so on, and it was like a private audience, you see.

But the fellow wanted us to rehearse what we were going to do, each child, you see. So now, when it came to my time, I had to -- I sang -- I had to sing that Morton Downey and, like I said, a little bit of Paul Robeson. But I didn't know all the song, the words on the Paul Robeson song.
So he said, 'Well, you wouldn't have to do that. Do you do anything else?' So I says, 'Well, I sing like Kate Smith.'
Now, he was a new announcer. So he wasn't familiar with the children's performing.
Where had you heare these performers?

Well, in Fitzgerald, Georgia, a lady used to play a record. She had a graphinola, and she used to let me play records, you know. I used to run errands for her. She liked White Castle hamburgers, was a nice old lady, she was, and she says that her husband was in import -- export and import, whatever. And he had all these kind of records, and she would let me -- that was kind of like a tip, you know.

But she loved them -- those White Castle hamburgers. At that time I think they was about seven cents a piece, two for 12 cents, something like that, they had. And she was letting me play these records, you see. And I got familiar with these different people, singers, the famous ones, you know, and I heard all of them at that time -- Ethel Waters, as I said, and Morton Downey, and I even heard the famous Irish singer -- what's his name -- and Caruso, Enrico Caruso at the time, you know.

But I mean, you know, I couldn't sing like him, you see, because he was -- I heard Duke Ellington -- he was with the McKinney's Cotton Pickers at the time. So I think I got jazz oriented from listening at those records, you see, recordings. And --
You were very young then.
Yeah, I was very young, but I was large for my size, because, see, my mother kind of set a record

when I was born, see. I was born four and a half pounds overweight, see. I was 12 and 1/2 pounds at birth. That's generally -- the normal, see, at birth was 8 and 1/2 pounds. That was considered a healthy baby, see. So -- so anyhow this announcer was saying, 'Well, what are you doing singing like Kate Smith, you know? That's a woman, you know.'

I liked Kate Smith better than anybody, you know. I thought her voice was so beautiful, you see. And I could actually sing just like her, you know. And where I was fascinated about it was because I knew all the words, the 'When the Moon Comes Over the Mountain,' you see.
(Laughter)
And -- there you go. Yeah.
(pause in the recording)
So you were just finishing up -- you were about to sing 'The Moon Goes Over the Mountain.'

Yes. But as I was saying, the announcer, he was a new announcer. I guess he was special for all the royal family from Buckingham Palace. They had just come over, I mean, you know, and this private audience.

Well, sorry to say, but that's when ABC and this -- this -- me, myself, at that time I was known as little Christopher, see? And on the 'Children's Hour' -- so anyhow, they figured out something for me to do. I just got a chance to do Morton Downey and a little bit of Paul Robeson, you
see. And that was it for me, you see.

And anyhow I met the -- they were children then, the royal family, like the -- Margaret and little Charles, you see. I met them. And I learnt the meaning of curtsy and so forth, which my mother had told me before, you know. That's the royal family; you have to curtsy. It's a curtsy, so -- you can't act (inaudible) at the royal family like you do ordinary people in the street, you see. You're keeping company, say, they're very special people, and, you know, kings and queens and so forth, you know.

There'll be governesses there and so forth, which there were, you see. So as I say, after that, because this announcer insisted, because I was a boy, I shouldn't impersonate a girl's voice or something, you know, I guess, and the -- at that time, you know, Kate Smith's singing was my favorite, you know.

And they got my notice, you see. I had to quit. I didn't want to work for the radio people any more. So my mother advised me not too. If I wasn't pleased with it, not to do it, because I didn't have to do it. I was young, --
How old were you?
-- still a minor, you know. I was going on seven at that time.
And what exactly was the problem?
Well, the problem was because he

insisted I not sing like Kate Smith, because she was a woman. Actually, I was embarrassed, you know, because I knew everybody loved Kate Smith, you know, at that time. See, she was known as America's sweetheart, you see. And --
So you never did any dancing for them? You hadn't danced as of yet?
No, I didn't dance as of yet, no. That came after. When I first danced was with Tiger Flowers.
But your mother always had ambitions for you as a --
As a singer.
-- singer?

Right, uh-huh, very, very strict about that. You know, she thought it was something in my voice, I could sing, you know, and was going to grow up to be a big concert singer like Paul Robeson or someone, you know, Enrico Caruso, you know, famous voices, you know.
And evidently that didn't happen, because further on up the road --
(Laughter)

-- I was walking up the street one day. You see, I had a way, you know, I didn't like to wear shoes outdoors, see. And I would -- I'd dress me up in the house, put on my shoes and (inaudible) learn how to tie -- you're a big boy now, you know, put your own shoes on, tie your shoes, you know,

but they'd make sure that it's did, you know. "Come here; let me look at you, you know. My mother's mother or something, you know -- and, all right, don't go too far away from the house, you know. Yes, ma'am, thank you, ma'am, yes, ma'am." And as I'd go out, you see, I could go out of my house two different ways, you see. You could come down on Houston Street -- that's the longest stairs. Or you could go at the back of the building and come down on Hilliard Street, you see.

And right there on Hilliard Street I'd take my shoes off and the socks, put them in the shoes, put them behind the door. And I'd come traipsing out barefooted, you see, all clean and everything, you know. Like And one day I come out there, and my little playmates, they hadn't arrived. I didn't see any of them, so I figured I'd go off and look for one of them, something.

And I stepped out off the curbstone, and there happened to be -- like I think it was a Coca-cola bottle top, something, you know, or stopper, you see, called them, and it had a little tar or something on the inside of it. And as I stepped down, you know, I thought I had stepped on some glass or something, and it didn't hurt, you know, and I kept walking.
But as I put my foot down, I would hear this sound, (clop, clop, clop). Uh-huh, so I thought to myself, wait

till I see my playmates, you understand. I'm going to make him mad, particularly, you see, I was very playful at that time. And so, sure enough, that's what happened. I figured, I said I'd look for some more of these bottle tops, and I could find where the tar was soft, you know, and put -- put back the tar inside and step on them with the other foot, see? Now, I'm barefooted, see, (inaudible) bottom of my foot, you see.

So soon enough eventually the playmates come out. It was a little store there right -- where I lived -- Grossman's grocery store, see, and we used to sit right alongside of it, you see, like a little curbstone off the building. We'd sit there. It would be about 12 of us or so. And so I see. They laughed and all, and I used to could turn a handspring, you know, stand on my hands, you know, and walk on my hands till you get your foot up against the wall, and then I'd ta-ka-ta-ta-ta-ta my foot, you see.
Hey, what kind of feet has he got, you know. And I'm just with this. I'm happy about it because I know -- I like to see people get -- try to figure out something, understand, you see. So --
(Laughter)
-- some of them said, you know what? You know, he should talk to J. D. That's what my partner's -- was called as -- he was known as J. D. They'd call people by their initials,

you know. His name was James Walker. But -- and I was Chuckles. And he was known as the South's (Inaudible) favorite son. And I didn't know why this was, but we used to see him, you know, and every time we would see him, he would be with his mother.

But he'd dress different. He had on a nice, pretty coat, you know, suit, pretty shoes and hat, tie and (Inaudible). I mean he wasn't -- he wasn't too surprised -- I wasn't too surprised, because my father was a great tailor, you know, and he made beautiful clothes, you know.
He was known as what?
Huh?
What was he known as? You said he was known as --
J. D., his initials, J. D.
You mean Chuckles or his father?
No, Chuckles. He gave an expression, known as --
Yeah, J. D.
Oh, the South's favorite son.
The South's?
Yeah, favorite son, yeah, because he had been -- he had been winning these amateur contests at the 81 Theater. He would always win the first prize, and he was a tap dancer, you know.
Was he older than you?

Oh, yeah, one year older. But he like -- he didn't associate with us, you know, other children. You know, we'd never see him playing with other children, anything. He was always with his mother, you know. And we eventually met her, you know.
But he was known as sort of an actor type in some way? He was admired by the kids?

Yeah, he was admired by kids, adults and everybody else. That's how he became known as the South's favorite son. That's how they would introduce him in the amateur show, you know. And the people, you could hear the audiences saying that, 'Wonder what he -- wonder what old J. D. going do tonight. I be glad when he dance, or something -- I like to see him dance, you know. The people in the South, they loved tap dancing, you see.

And the audiences are talkative, you know, and happy people. Hospitality is a way of life in the South. That part of it at least -- and, well, my little playmates really said that -- he should meet J. D. and try to get J. D. to teach him how -- ask J. D. to teach him some steps, you know, some dance steps, you know.

And they called me Boodgie, you see. And I said, 'Oh, but, gee, he wouldn't like me. I mean -- what kind of -- J. D. (inaudible) to play with us, you know?' So one fellow

said, 'Oh, yeah, he's very nice. I met him, you know, say -- all the children knew he was over on the stage, you see, and that was -- there was kind of happiness with him. They was kind of proud of him, you see. And that part of the city was known as Fourth Ward in Atlanta, Georgia.

And so eventually one day we was talking about him, and he happened to come up the street by himself, Hilliard Street, you see, and (inaudible) and (inaudible), 'Oh, here comes J. D., you know. I think it was John Peters that said it, 'Here come J. D. Said, 'What you going to say to him? Let's talk to -- let's ask him something, you know. Let's ask him about could he teach or help Boodjie with his -- teach Boodjie some tap dancing,' because my cousin was sitting there, first cousin, my Aunt Mary's son, Boby, you see, Boby Green. His name was James also, you see.

So sure enough, J. D. turned out to be a lovable person, you know. He had to be lovable, a little boy like that walking his mother, you know, and he was actually like a little man, you see. And he was very nice. So he set down with us. 'What you all -- what you fellows -- what you -- what are you all doing?' you know?

Right -- what have you been playing, you know? So we said something, well, we used to shoot marbles, you know. We was tossing bottle tops and so on and so on and so on. And they called it lag, you know, what you call pitching the
pennies, coins to the curb and stuff like that.

And he had a little song he used to sing, 'oh, the monkey wrapped his tail around the flagpole, showed his flagpole to the crowd, you know. And, you know, he was a cute little fellow, you see. Well, we all, we get to be friends easily. Children always do, right?

So my cousin asks him, says, 'Say, J. D., your name's James, right?' So he says, 'Uh-huh.' He had a funny way of talking too, Chuckles. That's J. D. -- used to say, he said, 'This is my first cousin, Boodjie, you know. Let's go here, Boodjie, says, show J. D. what you just did. Just do a little of it, you know.

And so I stand on my hands, you know, and ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta, and walk to the wall, pat my feet up against the wall, standing on my hands, you know, and I make this sound with the bottle tops on the bottom of my feet, you know, tick-a-tick-a-tick-a-tick-a-tick-a-tick, tick-a-tick-a-tick-time, tick. And I push myself away and land on down, bum-bum-bum-bum, you know.

And he liked that. He laughed, you know, ha-ha-ha-ha, ha-a, ha-ha-ha-ha, said, 'he dances,' you know. So Boby said, 'oh well, (inaudible) you dance, you know, to me. He could dance (inaudible). You live around here?' You know -- you know how children are. He said, 'Yeah' -- (inaudible) right upstairs there, his right upstairs up there,
looking out the window, you know.

So J. D. look up -- oh, yeah, that's (inaudible) uh-huh. He said, "Say, what you all want me to do? He said, "Well, could -- could you teach him one of them dances, them dance steps that you do, what they like to dance now, you know?" So J. D. said, "Well, yeah, I could teach him, you know, maybe teach him something sometime." He didn't set no definite time about it so I could (inaudible) explain to him how you supposed to do the dance steps, you see.

So I said, "Oh, yeah, that would be good. I would like to learn (inaudible) because I likes the way you -- I saw you dance. You won the first prize, you know, all excited. You know how children are. Yeah, he sure did, they said, sure did. How's your mother, this, that and the other -- (Laughter and inaudible remarks) And that make J. D., you know, he like us better. He's looking from one to the other, you know. And he was sort of like I was. He liked to make children laugh, you see. And he says, "All right, he says. "I can't stay away from home too long. I have to go right back, you know. I have to go back home. Nice meeting you fellows, you know, "I'll see you again."
And now, what he used to do, he used to go in the back yard of this -- somebody done throw the door somewhere, throw the door away, wooden door, and he used to put it
in the backyard, and he'd get out there and practice. That's how he taught himself to tap dance (inaudible) as he did, you see. And so he left. So much for that.

But he came back, and he was explaining to me how to do such and such a step, how to be on the beat, how to be on time with it. I liked that. And I liked that. Everything I would say "I like that, I like that, you know, see. I was learning. I could learn quickly, quick learner, you could call it.

So then one day, one afternoon there, here come Tiger Flowers walking across the street. Now, he was popular. He was the lightweight champion of the world at that time, Tiger Flowers, and he lived right just around the corner on Irving Street. And he says, he came walking right over across the street where we were sitting at, you know, and he said --
(Tape Two.)
Yes, anybody does that when they get, you know, (inaudible).
Chuck Green, tape two.
Goody, goody gumdrop.
(Laughter)
I'm full of laughter because this is a happy time in my life, you see. As I said, along came Tiger Flowers, and he -- as he crossed the street, which was Hilliard Street, he crossed

the street where we -- my playmates and I and my first cousin Boby, he was James Green. So he said, "I wants a dance teacher," you know. He knew we loved him, you see. Everybody in the world, I mean, in that city at least, loved Tiger Flowers, you see.

So he says, says to one of them -- I think he says to -- he says to my cousin Boby, you know, Boby was like -- he was kind of like a joker in playing cards, you understand. He was always doing comedy or something. And Tiger Flowers says, "Oh, no, not you." He stood up, you know, and said, "Oh, no, not you."

And he must have liked my color or something, you know. I was full of sunshine, tan, you see, I want to tell you -- (inaudible) so he said -- he says, "How about you?" you know. I was kind of serious at that time. I didn't -- I didn't laugh a lot myself but I was full of happiness, you understand. So he say, "Would you like to teach me? You know?"

So I look at Boby, you know, and my cousin Boby started shoving my shoulder (inaudible) that's Tiger Flowers (inaudible), thought I was going to make a million dollars or something teaching Tiger Flowers how to tap dance, you know. So really my idea was to teach myself along with teaching him, you see, because he says, how he was going to pay. "You teach me and I'll teach you, you know.
So everybody knew what that meant. If he teach me

how to fight like he did, I would be a champion or something, right. Well, that wasn't my ambition. So I didn't know what I wanted to be, and I was just trying to be head of the house, you know, because my father was away.

So anyhow he appointed me to meet him where he trained at in the YMCA down on 12th Street in Atlanta, Georgia, in the auditorium. So I went down there, and he started to doing some skipping rope, you know. You know, to box, the fighters skip the rope, you know, whew, whew, whew, wht-t, whew, and it was so pretty, the rhythms, you know.

And, oh, man, I was enjoying that myself. I was fascinated, you see. So then he said, 'So much for that.' He went over to the light bag, punching bag. He punched that. rerr-rerr-rerr-rerr, come to barbells and push them things out and on and on, he's coming; he'd run around, you know. Then he got the medicine ball, you know, and he said, 'Could you -- try to hit me with this,' you know.

It's a big leather -- leather ball, big thing, you know, and you pick it up. It wasn't so heavy, you know. You could throw it too. And that was -- he was teaching himself self -- art of self defense, right? So -- so he says, 'So much for that.' He says, 'How do you like that?' You know? And I says, 'That's fine. You hear them sounds?' You hear it while he was doing it. I said all this. I'm so excited, you know.

So he liked to make children happy, Tiger Flowers, very lovable person. Everybody loved him. So he said, 'Now, I'm ready.' He said, 'What's my first dance?' So in the meantime my Aunt Edna Bisson, she had done taught me how to do what -- what all dancers had to do at that time, know how to do. It was called a time step.

So that's what I started off to teaching him. Now, he liked that, you know. He was very pleased. So we was in there for about an hour, hour and a half or so, you know, and he was promising me this, that and the other, when I get a little older and to mention his name, and he said, 'You tell people if they ask you who you are, you say you're a little Tiger Flowers, you know, and you'll always have respect, you see?'
(Interruption in the recording)

You tell me about the -- I think I have -- the other part of this history in my life, fortunately, Mr. Tiger Flowers, he taught me all these -- important people's names in the fight -- in the prize fighting business at the time, and there was one gentleman named George Roby, which was Miss Lucille Achet's father-in-law. Now, Miss Lucille Achet, she used to have a record shop next door to the 81 Theater.

Now, that was Tom Bailey's theater, and it was just off five points in this city, Atlanta, Georgia, which the people there used to pride themselves on saying it was little New York City, you know, although I don't think there were

too many of them that (inaudible) would have actually visited New York City, but they would always see New York City in a lot of the films, the moving pictures that they show, you know, and, well, sure enough, after school -- I still went to school, you see, David T. Howard, and I was getting good grades, you know. But after school I would go and try to earn some money, you know, because my father was away.

And there was three ladies in my mother's -- well, it was three ladies with my mother's mother. It was two of her daughters and her and I living there on Houston in -- Hilliard Street in Atlanta, Georgia, in the Fourth Ward.

So I finally went up to -- like I was saying, they come up to this school, and whoever was in the head of the class, they would always get chosen to do something, some kind of chore that would be helpful to them in their education.

So one day there some newspaper people from a very popular newspaper in that city was called The Constitution. They were there, some, you know, some publisher, editor, like that. And I would always happen to be in the head of the class, --

Yes, it was.

Right.

It was called the Beaulah Theater, and she -- she sold it to some white people, and they changed the name of it -- the theater to the Dallas Theater, you see.

And because she used to travel, you know, in the South, and she was a great singer, beautiful voice, very good singing. I think she's the only one Bessie Smith ever complained about, you see, because she sang some song -- I think it was 'Syria' or something she sang, and Bessie Smith used to sing the same song. But -- no disrespect, but I think Ella B. Moore had a prettier voice than Bessie Smith, you see.

But, see, she used to calk up. She used to blackface. She was a woman, a female blackface comedian, because that's what he was, Chinch Moore, you see. I say they were of course stars. It was their show, because they had had the Brown Skin Models, number one. Then they had Brown Skin Models number two, and then they had Brown Skin Buddies, and that was the last of the shows. Then they was going to stop doing the shows, you see.
And was this in fact their last show?
Yes. See --
You said it was a variety show, a review.
Review.
What kind of things were in the review?
Oh, everything, even butter beans and Sousa was in the show, you know.
Were there other dancers?
Yeah.
Tap dancers?
Yeah. Eddie Rector, he was in it, Brown Skin Buddies, Eddie Rector, Faustin Beatty, yeah, what you call it, the Four Gob's, you had Sonny and Full Dobbs, Suddy Austin, Eddy Vinton.
Was this the same time that you were dancing that these people were with them?

Well, they weren't with them anymore. See, they finished that week at the 81 Theater. That was the finish of it, see, and they announced that they were going to marry. See, they were going to become husband and wife. See, they had been like partners for about seven years, you know, male and female partners, see, and that's the kind of act they did, see. And he -- Mr. Chinch Moore, he used to do these songs like That's Life, Pick Up the Pieces, I'm Busted, things like that, you see. And she would sing songs, you see, and --
(Laughter)

-- like a husband and wife, you see, because he was supposed to be out of work, trying to get a job, and he had a pint of whiskey, empty pint whiskey bottle, you see. Now, an empty pint whiskey bottle like you -- you get a nickel deposit on it, you see. You have to leave a nickel deposit on the bottle, and you return the bottle, you get a nickel deposit.

You see?
So that's what their routine was consisted of, him going out in the mornings trying to get a job, see? And the music would be playing these -- like vamping, you know, an introduction to the song. And she would like ask him -- whatever she called him, Moore, or whatever name she called him -- says, 'You going to work today, going get a job?' You know? And he would start to singing one of these songs, you know, like 'I'm Busted.' He needed to have streetcar fare or something to go down and look for work, you see.

And what he'd do, he'd try to get some money from her, because that was -- this was before prohibition, see, 1925, see. Prohibition then come in, and so they were selling bootleg whiskey, see. Now, Chinch, he used to take the money and he'd go to the bootlegger and get some -- a certain amount of whiskey in his pint bottle, you see.
(Laughter)

That's what it consisted of, see. That's how they would get into these songs.
See, because when he'd come back, he'd be kind of tight. He'd be kind of drunk, intoxicated, see. And she would ask him, uh-huh, 'Did you get a job?' And then he would start to singing this song, words like 'That's Life' or something, you know.
This was, I guess, hilarious to
the audience, of course.
Yes, tremendous comedy, really was.
So there was a whole dramatic structure to it, of him trying to find a job and her scolding him each time that he didn't get a job?
Satirical --
Right. Right. He had to explain why he didn't get no work or something, you know.
Uh-huh. And it all revolved also around the illegal act of going and get liquor. It was illegal. You weren't supposed to do that.
Yeah, he been to the bootlegger's, yeah.
(Laughter)
Okay. Do you remember any of those particular lines that they used to have or those particular jokes?

Yeah, well, that's what I'm saying. I mean the comical part of it was when he would mention some fictitious employer, some name, you know, but he's trying to tell his wife that -- how important this employer is, and he's Mr. Big, you know. Very important man, That employer, lot of money and this, that and the other thing and she would say to him, 'Well, it's funny you never -- when you come back in, you haven't given me nothing, and he -- and he would go into another song, you know, about 'I'm Busted', you know.

Other words, he let the cat out of the bag by explaining that he don't have no money, you understand. See, sometimes he would say, well, I worked at the end of my first four hours or something, you know, and she would say, well, what about the pay, you know, and he would go into his song, you see -- I'm Busted.

So now that's -- see, but he would always -- his bottle would be empty, you know, and he'd have a corner in it, and he would hide it under the back porch steps, you know, then and he'd go up the steps, and he'd do some comedy going up the steps, you know, like staggering and so forth, and he'd knock on the door -- whack, wack, wack, wack, wack.

And the door would fly open -- bam -- and there she's standing there with the black face, you know, and big eyes, 'It's you; what took you so long?' You know. And she start -- he started to backing back down the steps, you know.
(Laughter)
You understand? You get the picture?
So but -- (RECORDING INTERRUPTION)
(Inaudible) important line.

Yeah, you see, that was a way of life, you see. It was actually a reality because these bootleggers, the law was after them, you see, what they call the revenooers or something, you see. And Mr. Moore, Chinch Moore, you see, they based their routines on these realities of life, ways of
life, you see. And that's what made it so comical, because -- pardon me, please.

And the money, they had money called the bow dollar then, you know.

(Laughter)
And that's what we were trying to get, you know. Sometimes people would -- they would take and wrap the money up in --

So we had an agreement. We said, 'Well, yeah, yeah,

we'll do that. We'll do that. Go to sleep now. Go to sleep now. So we'd go to sleep, because they would always look in the room and see if we're asleep or not, you know, something, you know. We'd put our heads under cover and make like we're asleep or something, you see.

And my mother used to go over to a place called Summer Hill. That's on the west side in Atlanta, Georgia. So finally mother come home, you know. I used to meet her at the streetcar, you know, stop there on Hilliard Street, going towards Highland Boulevard, you know. She was glad to see me and all, you know, but my mother wasn't well.

Now, adults have a way of covering up, you know. They don't let you know -- a little child know how bad off they are, see, and I think mother was on the way of dying, but I didn't know. How old were you then?
Well, I was going on nine years old then.
And --

Right, yeah. Yeah.

Yes. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, uh-huh.

the train, and Mr. Robey bought this car. And --
Excuse me. That was -- Chuckles was with you?
Yeah, just Chuckles, you see, because --
What happened to --

Shorty, well, he didn't -- he got to be a ladies' man, you know. He was -- very handsome kid, he was, and like old women like, you know, they liked him, you know, and he took advantage of it. He was that type of child, you see. And he didn't want to leave. So it was Chuckles and I, see.

Sure enough. It took us about seven and a half weeks to get to Philadelphia, you see, because we was always stopping. We had the worst looking car on the highway, you see. It was called a Model T, you see. (Laughter)

fast, and then the engine would catch up, you know. Then we'd get in our Model T and drive up and catch up, you know, follow them along, see if they don't break down again or something. So we made a lot of friends like that on the way up.

Yeah, just us three. This guy, Obi, and like Slim and Shorty, see.

-- that was taking you to New York?

No --

(Recording interruption) So we met Mr. Billy Pierce -- Mr. and Mrs. Billy Pierce rather -- and he put us in Mr. Buddy Bradley's studio, where Mr. Buddy Bradley used to teach. And we stayed there in the studio for about -- about two weeks, you see, and I met Miss Eleanor Powell there. She was a student of Buddy Bradley, and I -- something good happened for her, see. She was captain of the chorus line at the Paramount Theater there in New York City, and she used to come up to 46th Street, you know, between shows and take lessons from Mr. Buddy Bradley.

But by him not being there, she saw me. I was asking Slim another question about tap dancing, and she told Mr. Pierce that she had gotten a break or something to the moving picture people. They wanted her to make a movie or something. This was without a screen test. You know, it was a rush job or something, and she would have to learn sound, you know, tap dancing.

She was already a great dancer. She was a champion dancer, but she had never did like the sound with the taps, you know, and she hadn't --- really hadn't put taps on her shoes. She had some favorite pair of shoes she liked to dance in. So she was getting taps on these shoes at the time that Mr. Buddy Bradley left. He went to England and Europe, you see.

And quite naturally, I don't think she knew this, and -- but she still liked to learn these things, this tap dancing, see. So she showed me some of the steps that -- rather she chose me. She asked Mr. Pierce, say, I like the way he dances, that one over there. She probably thought I was a teacher, you see. I was asking a question about tap dancing from my partner, Slim. See?
Well, you were just a little kid then, weren't you?
Yeah, I was a teenager. And, see, because we had aged some. We had stayed in Philadelphia with Edwina Sutton about two and a half years, at So, I was
approximately about 15 years old. I was going into the 15th year.
But, of course, you were progressing with your tap dancing all the time. I mean You just didn't sit around, I mean --

No. No. No, we danced, you know, because it was right in a dancing studio, you know, so we danced, learned new steps and things, and I was -- I was in that process at the time she looked over in the corner and saw me, see, and she says she wanted -- she liked the rhythm. Evidently, I must have been a natural dancer or something, you know, because I was in the process of learning how to dance on roller skates too, you see. I could tap dance on roller skates, and I was very --
Versatile.

-- versatile, see, at that time, see. But I -- I couldn't understand. I was trying to understand myself, you see, and I knew I loved rhythm. I knew -- I knew that. I loved rhythms. That's why she chose me, and she -- he gave her permission to take the lessons from me, you see, so -- for Mr. Buddy Bradley, see.

So she showed me some of the steps. She said she had never used taps on her shoes before, and for me to watch and see what I thought of it and could I finish up some of the routine. And she explained that she had to be in Hollywood
in two weeks, you see. So --
This is before Eleanor Powell had learned any tap dancing? This was her first introduction to tap dancing?
Yes, that was it. See, she was taking from Mr. Buddy Bradley.
So you initially went to New York and were hanging around the Buddy Bradley-Billy Pierce Studio?
Yeah, Billy Pierce Studio, you see.
How long were you hanging around there before Eleanor Powell came in?
Oh, about two -- two days. She came in about the third day we were there, you know.

Well, maybe -- well, tell me the story about Eleanor Powell, but I'm interested in what was -- what was the Buddy Bradley-Billy Pierce Studio like? First tell me the Eleanor Powell story. What happened with that and what you taught her?

Well, I taught her -- I taught her about a chorus and a half of how she could tap -- she could do like the same ballet and put the taps to the ballet, you see. See, because she was a champion ballet -- tap -- ballet dancer. She was really was a champion. You could understand everything she did, even if you never did any ballet yourself or anything, you know.

Well, my mother's dance teacher was also a ballet dancer, you know, and she was some kind of an authority of that dance. And so I understood it. But I explained to Eleanor Powell how she could get rhythm with the ballet, and she wouldn't have to, you know, not do ballet dancing, see, because, I mean, these spins and pivots and pirouettes and things, you know, and leaps, anything, see, told her how she could get the taps in there. So that's what I was teaching her, you know.
Which you will notice, when she dances, she does lots of turns with taps on, tap turns, which -- a girl, you know, (inaudible) would have to have ballet to be able to do pirouettes.
Was this something that you choreographed yourself in terms of the amount of taps?
Yeah. Yeah.
Can you demonstrate to show me what those taps were like? In a turn? Or what exactly -- what rhythms did you show her?

Yeah, well, I showed her how to do snatches, you see. See, in ballet there's a snatch, what they got -- I call it a snatch because it is --it really is a preparation for a pivot, you see. Now, one foot goes out. The left foot goes out, and it comes back to the right foot, and then a spin occurs. A pivot occurs.
Well, that's what I showed her, how to do, add sound to this. As the foot go out, you know, she can make a sound, you know, like --
(Tap interlude)

-- like that, you see. And then cross over with the right foot and then convey the pivot, see, because she could actually, when she spinned, she could spin like -- she'd go around six times. By the time an ordinary person would turn once, she could spin about six times with the head, you know, one, two, three, four, five six, like that, and I heard the beat. I could see the beat actually, you know. And I knew it was a sound. So that's what I was teaching her, you know.

And I still do one of the steps I taught her. I even do it now, I mean, and I do a dance to the melody of 'Caravan,' you see, that's a Duke Ellington melody, and I do some of the Eleanor Powell tap in that, see, that I taught her for Mr. Buddy Bradley, because he wasn't there.
Now, that was a job that Mr. Pierce, Billy Pierce gave me, see I could be like a Buddy Bradley assistant dancer, see. You know, but --
Were there other assistants also working then?
Yeah, well, it was one guy in there, but he was an undeveloped dancer too, I mean, Henry LeTang. See, (inaudible), See, and Eleanor Powell, she discontinued Henry LeTang's lesson, because

she was in a hurry. She had to learn something quick, you know. So she was pleased with the idea of -- she could inject her ballet into tap dancing, because she thought that would be more impressive. See, they allowed her to make the movie without a screen test, you know. That's what a great -- that's how great a dancer she was.
So you initially taught her how to tap?

Well, yeah, then first -- I actually finished, like attached on to what she had learned. She showed me what she had learned from Buddy Bradley without the taps on, but it was actually tap dancing, see, but she didn't -- she liked these shoes. I'm telling you it was a favorite shoe. Dancers was like that in those days. They had a favorite pair of shoes that they liked to dance in. You understand? So by the time she got the taps on to the shoes, Mr. Buddy Bradley, he had left, you know. He had caught the boat and gone to England, see. And so I just did that, you know --
(Recording interruption)
Okay, why don't you explain to me a bit about the Buddy Bradley-Billy Pierce Studio, what it was like.
Well, it was the most famous dance studio in New York City at that time. This was in 1931, the

first of 1931, in February. See, because people like George M. Cohen -- by the way, James Cagney was teaching on the third floor also. He was a dance teacher in the Billy Pierce Studio, and he had students like Dan Dailey, Van Johnson, even James Stewart, he used to come there, see. And they -- they became very famous in moving pictures, you see, these people, which also happened to Eleanor Powell and Arlene Judge, Rita Hayworth, Lucille Ball, Joan Blondell -- she used to come there -- and Nancy Carroll, she was famous in the movies, Warner Brothers movie star.

And I think a friend of mine, Mr. Buddy Bradley's wife, you know, widow, Lady B. Bradley, she explained to me about Clifton Webb, you see. He was also a student of Buddy Bradley, and he was very popular. You know, George M. Cohen, he was a very popular man, famous for composing songs, putting on Broadway shows and all this, and that's really what Mr. Buddy Bradley was involved in at the time he left for England, because he was doing the choreographies for these great shows, these Broadway shows, and they weren't giving him the credits, you know, like someone -- I think they called him Busby Berkeley, and he was not a dancer, but he had Mr. Buddy Bradley doing the choreographies for those dance numbers in the movies, and he didn't give him credits, you know.
And so I think that's why Mr. Billy Pierce allowed Buddy Bradley to take this vacation like trip, you know. He
called it a rest, said he needed a rest because he was kind of overworked.
What was the relationship with -- between Billy Pierce and Buddy Bradley?
Well now, that was a teacher and employer, you see. It was the Billy Pierce Studio --
Billy Pierce discovered Buddy.
Yeah, see, yeah --

Billy Pierce gave Buddy his first opportunity to teach. He had this idea of so many of the white performers needing this sort of rhythm dancing, and he gave Buddy his first opportunity with -- somebody, Irene Delroy -- she was in a show, in the Greenwich Village Follies, something like that. I hope I'm right.

And he asked Buddy -- Buddy, I think he was about 18 at the time -- if he thinks he could put a number together for Irene Delroy, which he did. He'd never done it before, but he just had this gift of making a girl look very cute with taps, without looking sort of hefty or awkward. And he taught her this little number, and she went back into the show, stopped the show, and that's what caused the influx of white show biz peoples at that time going to the Billy Pierce Studios and everybody wanting these hit numbers that stopped shows, naturally.
So that's really what started the fame of the Billy
Pierce Studios.
So you took a liking to Buddy Bradley and he took a liking to you, and that encouraged you to come up to his studio from Philadelphia?
Yeah.
Well, where did you stay when you were in New York?
The Belvedere Hotel. That's until Nat Nazarra and Buck and Bubbles came along.
Uh-huh. So you were staying along with Chuckles?
Yes.
You two were staying alone at the hotel?
Right, yes.
You were only how old at that time?

Well, we were teenagers, see. I was in my 15th year. Chuckles was 16. He was going into his 16th year. He was nine months older than I, and, as I was saying, we had the name of Shorty and Slim, you see.
(Laughter)

See, but to work -- to work on the stage, we still weren't allowed to go on the stage unless we had guardian, you know, of some sort like that, and Mr. Robey, he was -- he was a fight you see promoter, and he wasn't actually in show business.
Well, were you working on the stage at this point?
No, sir.
At all? So you hadn't actually performed in front of an audience since the time when you were with the --

This charity show in Philadelphia at the Hippodrome Theater there at that time. They had one in Philadelphia, and they had one over here on Third Avenue in New York City, you see. And -- we were like aging, you see. Mr. Robey was supposed to come back like in -- and he would -- we were supposed to stay with him like until we became of age like, you see.

But that didn't happen because Nat Nazarra came along, see. He was looking for a Little Buck'n Bubbles at that time. He already had the original Buck'n Bubbles. They were great stars. They were the biggest colored stars we had at that time besides like, see, because Bert Williams, he was the first one. That was Williams and Walker. They were very famous.
Had you met Williams and Walker up to this point?
No, sir, I never met them at all, see. I saw Mr. Williams once in Zigfield Follies with Will Rogers, see, and we became great friends before he died. Mr. Will
Rogers, he taught me to rope dance, and I still got the mark in my hand now from twirling the rope, you know.
(Laughter)
He was a very nice man, you know. Everybody liked him too, see. And he used to come there, used to come to the studio, Billy Pierce Studio, you know. And --
So you had been at the studio for how long before you met Buckin' Bubbles?
Well, I was there going into the third week, you see. It was.

It did. It really did. Well, Mr. Bradley said this would happen, you know, see. He said we had great personalities, see.

Yes. Yes.

Well, we did -- well, my partner, he eventually learned to play the vibraphones, you see, and he did later --
This was prior to the time you were
Chuck and Chuckles -- as Slim and Shorty when you were in Philadelphia, what kind of things would you do that made people like you?

Well, we were so playful, you see. We'd dance, you know, and we made little funny mannerisms, you see. And like I say, I could turn the handspring. See, that was like what you call the punch step, call -- it's actually a trick, you know, of entertaining, you see, and --
That's the word; they were very entertaining, --
Yeah, --
-- because Chuck would play the vibra -- vibes.
Yeah, this was prior to that. He's talking about before.

Well, it's like --

I guess so. Natural -- natural dancer like, you see.
A flair for comedy?
Yeah, see, like -- like something like you know a person, you know everybody in the audience, like

you were great friends, you know. And it was like telling a story really, but it was on a -- it was in activities, you see. And as I say, Slim was a great tap dancer. He was a natural, see, because he taught himself all these tap dances that he knew, and he used to win the first prizes all the time.

He won the first prize eight times at the 81 Theater on -- then the time after I was there, I mean he won the ninth time, see. He was after a record. He wanted to win ten first prizes, you see. And he was so good until one time he had to pinch hit for one of the master of ceremonies, a fellow named Johnny Jazz' cousin. He had to go to Tennessee, something. His mother got sick or something. He had to go to Tennessee.

Moore, you see, and got us together, see.

But then getting back to New York, he continued to be a great tap dancer, and he was always learning me things, you know, something. I say, well, what would happen if we have to do some other tap dance, and what are we going to do? And we were in the process of teaching each other how to do --
place the steps and so forth, what to name the steps. See, Slim, when he would dance, if he'd do a step, he'd give the step a name, you know, like ride the horse or something like that, you know.
What would that -- what does that mean, ride the horse? What kind of step would that be made up of?
Well, you see, you do the rhythm of the horse's hoofs, you know, and you just do the mannerisms, the gesture, like you've got the reins.
Like how? Can you do it? Can you do a little?
Yeah, like that, see, like there you go, like it's really -- in taps it went like this.
(Tap dancing interlude)
That's ride the horse.
Yes, you can hear it.
See -- see --
What other names -- what other types of dances did he have that he gave names to? And did you give names to certain dances too?

Well, the steps he would do this. He'd give a step a name like, you know, like they say the scissors, see, like that, you know, thread the needle, things like that. See? He would just give a certain step that name, so instead
of saying like this, number one, number two, number three, he would say the name of the step. So that was just something between he and I.
You had your own language going for the steps that you --
That was it. That was it.
That's how you were able to put your numbers together, with your own language.
Yes. Yes.

Yes
At this time, Did you always have an act in mind that you were both going to be performing together as an act?
Yes.

No.
Okay.
Uh-huh.

No, no. They'd have one -- they wouldn't realize -- they didn't know -- I mean -- that he was such a

If I would do it correctly, he would sit there. If I'd do it incorrectly, he would get up and show me how to do it correctly, you see.

Yes.
He was more like the straight man in a certain way?
Yeah, he was the straight man. That was him, Chuckles, yeah.

Yeah, by -- about in the third week. Mr. Buck -- just Buck -- Nat Nazarra and Buck -- one of the Buck'in Bubbles.

Right.

That's it.

Yeah, well, there was a fellow, the twins' brother, he was Louis Brown. He used to come down there and practice. And there was a fellow named Johnny Dillman. He's a great musician now. He's a trumpet player. He plays trumpet. But he was a dancer at that time, you know. He's a dance teacher rather. He was the one that was up on the second floor in the Billy Pierce Studio, you know.
You know --
Ask that same question.

Wouldn't you say it wasn't that many black performers going in and out the Billy Pierce Studios? It was just mostly the people that worked as assistants or playing the piano? That's right. That's right. There was another colored gent that came in there named Buster Newman. See, he turned out to be a dance teacher, see. But like I say, the twins' brother, Louis Brown, he was about the only other Negro that was in there. He wasn't taking lessons. He was teaching himself. He was practicing there, you see.

Well, she was. That's what she does, you see, because she had the record shop there in Atlanta, Georgia, but I mean she was a very important woman. You understand? She's very popular. You see? I mean throughout the United States, you see, as a businesswoman, you see, and -- and through her father-in-Law, you know, and she was actually in the money world, you see, and important companies like record companies and so forth like that, theatrical people, she knew most of them, see? Cheerful stuff.

he said, "What tempo?" so we told him the tempo for it. We said, "Do you know 'Broadway Melody'?" and he said, "What tempo?" Bugle Call "Magic Hall Rag," and "What tempo?" So that's when we had to leave the Belvedere Hotel and go and move in with Mr. Nat Nazarr, because he was looking for a little Buck and Bubbles. He wanted to -- see, Buck and Bubbles was so popular, such great stars. They was big box office at that time, you see. Because I'm saying that America was overcoming the Depression at that time, so work was plentiful and the more the merrier. So that's when Mr. Nat Nazarr had the idea of injecting us into Buck and Bubbles' act, and that's what he did, see? But he trained us. He trained us for about two and a half years. He wouldn't allow us to go to Harlem. He wouldn't even allow us to go down into the Village. We were only allowed to go ten blocks in each direction, four directions, you know, and he lived on 48th Street then he had a bridge club where all the great magicians used to come. And we stayed up there with him.
So Nat Nazarr was at this point giving you a two year training.
Yeah.
To make you into an act, a good act.
Yeah. A little Buck and Bubbles.
You didn't perform during those two years or you did?
No.
What would he do, did he put you up in his house?
Yeah. We stayed there with him.
And he'd meet with you once a day and you'd go through your routine?
No, he'd like -- he trained us, you know. Some days we'd stay up all night. Saying one -- doing one line, you know.
Hard taskmaster.
You see, he was teaching us how to convey, like when you say a word, how to project.
Project.
See? Like he says, 'Hey boys, what you running for?' See, he was teaching us how to project, say talk, like Buck and Bubbles.
Did he train Buck and Bubbles in the same way?

I don't think so, no. No, he bought Buck and Bubbles from Ramon Navarro, see, they were under contract to Ramon Navarro, that's what he told us, and he bought the contract, see? Buck and Bubbles used to make them little movies, you know. When they was children, you see.
They was in his act. Nat Nazarra had a -- he was a world famous act, you know, Nat Nazarra and Sons, see. He had five sons, see? They had a balancing act, see?
He was perfecting your act.
Yes. Performing, you see, performing. He was perfecting that.
But he wasn't acting himself.

Oh Yeah. He was like what you call the -- he was the bottom man, see. His sons used to run up on his shoulders and on top of him, and he'd balance all of them up on his shoulders, you see. He showed us a scrapbook, you see, where he would pick up one son, be laying down with his hand out, and he'd reach down and grab his hand and pick him straight up, like that. Straight out.
So he actually had a sense of acrobatics himself.
Oh, he was a champion.
And was he giving you sort of pointers, in terms of acrobatic tap?

Yeah. Well, see, I was very proud of the handspring, see, and I was in the process of teaching myself how to tap dance with roller skates on. A few times there we worked -- they had a theater there where the Uris is. It was called the Capitol Theater. We worked in there with Buck and Bubbles. I danced with these roller skates on

and I had a little trick that I did where I'd inject the handspring with the roller skates on, and come down with the music, in time with the music, you see? And I must have exagerrated it in some way, because I overdid the handspring and come down, instead of landing on the skates I landed on the skates, but I had to go down and catch myself with my hands, like that, you see, over near the orchestra. It was the thing to -- like you're playing with the musicians, you see, do you know, like that, you know. "Hello." See? It was a little bit of comedy. But I mean, he was standing in the wings and he actually thought I had fell or something, you know, I was going to hit my head or something, you know. And it excited him you see, and that was the end of my roller skating tap dancing. He took it out, you see.
Because he was afraid you'd hurt yourself.
Yeah.
But you never really did hurt yourself doing it.
No.
Can you still do that today, by the way?
No. No. I never did it since then. That was all, see?
So you went through this intensive
two years of being trained by Nat Nazarro.
Right.
Now, in what kind of things did he train you, other than to project?

How to -- how to deliver. How to introduce ourselves to an audience, to come on stage how to exit, you know. See that was re-training, you see. But we already knew that from being with Chinch and Ella B. Moore, you know? So -- but his ideas was altogether different. He didn't want that. He wanted someone -- like I say, a little Buck and Bubbles. That's what he wanted. You understand?
Was he teaching you the same routines that Buck and Bubbles knew, or something completely different?

Just part of it. Just certain parts of the Buck and Bubbles act that we could repeat in the act because they was so funny. They'd say a line like, "What was you running up the street for?" And -- no, he'd say, "Where was you going with that old black goat I seen you with in the shopping district." "My black goat can give white milk." He'd say, "That ain't nothing." He said, "Can you do it?" And he'd say, "Well, I was going to the shopping district, the sporting center to get some golf shoes -- some knickers." And he said, "Well, what about the smell?" He said, "Oh, he'll get used to me." Things like that. He said, "What was you running up the street for the other day?" He said, "Oh, it looked like it was

going to rain out there and I didn't want to get wet." He'd say, "Oh, you wasn't afraid of getting wet. You was scared of the lightning." "Who's scared of lighting," he'd say. "You is." "The other day a thunderstorm come up, the lightning flashed, and you run down in a dark cellar and hid." He'd say, "Well, I've got to protect myself." He said, "Protect yourself? Don't you know if lightning is going to hit you it's going to hit you." Said, "Well, if lightning's going to hit me, leave it look for me." He said, "Well, what was you running up the street after that, I saw you a couple of days after that." He'd say, "Well, I was running to stop a fight." Say, "Yeah, who was fighting?" He'd say, "Me and another fellow." Say, "Well, what did you want to run for?" He'd say, "Well, you don't think my legs are going to stand around and see my body abused, do you?" He'd say, "Yeah, but the fellow soon caught up with you." He said, "He hit you, he knocked you down and I came over there to take up your part." Said, "Me and the fellow stood up over you and fought like two dogs worrying over a bone, and you wouldn't even get up and do anything." And Bubbles said, "Well, did you ever see two dogs fight over a bone?" And Buck said, "Sure, I did." "Well, did you ever see the bone get up and do anything?" So that's what we was -- he was training us to do, like certain things that he said.
Do you remember how the routines --
like how was the tap integrated into that? That was just comedy, but how was tap integrated into their act?
Well, I mean Bubbles tap danced in his act, but we couldn't -- we had our tap dances, was what Nat Nazarro saw us do, like "Sweet Sue" and "Broadway Melody" and "Bugle Call Rag", you see.
Well, was the comedy that you're talking about, was that comedy you would do, or was that comedy that Buck and Bubbles would do?

That was comedy that they would do, but we, by us being children like that, a little Buck and Bubbles, it was so funny if it was repeated, like if you heard a funny joke, and every time someone would repeat this joke, you would laugh, because it was just that funny, and they had a way of -- a delivery, a way of speaking, you see.
So you would repeat the jokes that they had already done.

Just some of them. Just some of them. Like run out -- we'd run through the -- like run out on the stage, like while they're out there, you know, and they would be looking, you know. Every time one of us would say something, you understand. It really was a comical idea.
The expressions, too.
Because Negros, at that time with the face, the eyes --
Yes, the expressions.

-- and all, you know. And he'd look -- when the other one would say something, he'd look over there, you know, and when the guy punched the line (Unintelligible) -- they'd jump back, you know, and the people would laugh.
They call that mugging.
Yeah. They call it mugging.
I'm interested in other routines that they used to do, other sort of comedy type things, and also the kind of tap that they did and the music that they performed to.
Their act was 42-1/2 minutes, see, Buck and Bubbles.
Uh-huh.

It was actually 39-1/2 minutes, but they had an encore, which was 2-1/2 minutes, you understand? Like they'd come out and bow, and they says -- they would both say, 'Ladies and gentlemen.' Then they would look at each other and one would say, 'Go ahead, you make the speech.' 'No, you make the speech.' 'I ain't going to make no speech.' Said, 'Well, I ain't going to make no speech.' 'Well, there ain't going to be no speech.' 'Well, why didn't you say that, Look you should have said that,' and, 'If I had known that,' and so forth. Then they'd go back off stage, arguing in the wings. So that was the encore.
Naturally funny.
Yeah. Natural, you see.
So they'd go off the stage arguing with each other about who was going to make the speech.
Yeah.
That was the encore, though.
Yeah.
What did their show open up with?
Oh, they opened up with like, 'Rhythm For Sale.' They had a special song written for Buck and Bubbles.
What was that like?
Oh, it was a pretty thing. (Singing), rhythm mad 'All the world is a beautiful thing,' like that.
What singing, and then -- not tap dancing.

But it's music. The music would be playing it. The music. That's the instrumental. That's to bring them on. And you'd see the curtain shake or something, you know, and Bubbles would back out. 'Come on. Push on the piano.' The piano would move a little more. He'd say, 'That's it, push, push on the piano.' And you'd see Buck with the cap on, lean way out, and he's almost laying down, you know.
Trying to push a grand piano.
Yeah. He'd look out from under the cap at the audience and he'd say, 'Well, you just pull your end.'

And he'd say, "My end will follow." And he'd get out there and they'd be looking at each other you know, and the music stops. Buck would snatch the stool off the piano, and wind it, wind it down, you know. He'd sit it down in front of under the piano keys, the keyboard, you know. Then he'd sit down on the piano stool, you know, and he started talking. And like he'd ask him a question, "What's your name?" "How do they call you?" "You got a dog?" "Yeah, I got a dog." "What's his name?" He'd say, "I calls him wagon wheel." "Why do you call him wagon wheel?" "Because he knows when I spoke." He'd say, "You got a dog?" He'd say, "Yeah, I got a dog." "What's your dog's name?" "I ain't named him yet." He said, "What you going to call him?" He said, "I think I'll call him Axle Grease." He'd say, "Why are you going to call him Axle Grease?" He said, "Because he knows when I got the bones." And he says -- and he asked him something else. He'd say something else to him. He'd say, "You know what?" He said, "If you had in your head what I've got in mine, you couldn't sleep at night." He said, "I had them, but I got rid of them." He said, "Ha, ha, ha." He laughed. "You know what," he says, "You should pull your curtains down, your window curtains down." "Why should I pull my window curtains down?" He said, "Because I saw you kissing your wife last night." He says, "Oh, no, I wasn't even at home last night." Things like that. He'd throw his cap at him. No, no. When

he'd look over there he'd see Buck laying with his head on his forearm, you know. And he said, "What's the matter, are you tired?" He said, "No, I ain't tired." He's still got his head on his arm. He said, "Well, what you laying down there for?" Said, "Just resting, so I won't get tired." Then he'd throw his cap at him and hit him. So Buck raised up and he'd pick up his cap and pick up the piano stool, then he'd walk over to where Bubbles is standing, like he's going to hand him his cap back. So when Bubbles reached for his cap, he dropped it on the floor. He says, "There's your cap. Pick it up." And Bubbles would look at the piano stool he's holding, you see? He'd say, "That's not my old cap. That's my new cap." He'd say, "Well, pick up your new cap, where I can bust you across your old head." "You aren't going to hit me with that." "I'm going to knock all of the yarn off of you with this." He said, "You know, this ain't no ham sandwich I've got in this pocket." And he'd hold out the piano stool and say, "Yeah, and this don't look like no sponge cake, either." He said, "I'll cut that stool off and leave your hand up there." He said, "Put that down. Put that down." Buck would walk back to the piano keyboard and put the stool down. Then they'd get into (Inaudible). And he says, "Play some music." He started playing on the keys and Bubbles would make like he's going to sing, you see. He'd sing something. (Singing), "Ah, sweet mystery of life --", and he'd look around and say, "Hey,
Okay let's just --

John Barner, that's one of Nat Nazarra's sons. What's the fellow that plays Mannix, O'Connor, he's another one, John Ireland. That's big brother John. He's one. And then there's Cliff Nazarra and Nat Nazarra, Jr. They're all alive. They're still alive.
And then -- well, the only one that's passed already is Mr. Buck. And, of course, Nat Nazarra, Sr., he passed some years ago. He passed in 1959, I think.

Yeah.

And then Buck be telling, he said, "Why, no. You -- we ain't supposed to be down here. We supposed to be up yonder in the buzzard's roof, you know. And he looked right at him when he said buzzard, see, because the buzzard's a real black bird, man. He's black as you can get, you know. understand"

(Laughter)

Well, that was actually authentic at that time. You know, that was -- they did -- some theaters did have that. They would have like whites downstairs, blacks upstairs. Understand? So (inaudible) they guess it was -- I don't know whose idea it was to have this, you know.

Terrific idea.
Yeah, he was a great show --
Terrific comedy.

No.
How -- how far before you had been introduced to them was this act --
Oh, goodness, that was many, many, many years, you know. Gees, I guess -- I wasn't even a teenager when that was happening.
Well, what kind of stuff did they do aside from that running and when the act was going on? Was that --major part of that act, or did they do other things?

Yeah, Well, they did -- like Mr. Bubbles -- they danced. They danced together. They used to tap dance together. See, I guess that's how we -- impression was laid on by Nazarra -- Chuckles and I done, you know. I mean Dancing to the 'Sweet Sue' and the 'Broadway Melody,' you see,
because Buck and Bubbles used to tap dance together, you know. See?
What kind of tapping did they do at that point?

Very good. Expert tap dancing. And Bubbles, he was called Crazy Legs. I don't know where he got -- you know, like skinny, skinny legs, you see, and he wore the pants up like on the shin like, you know. And he wear these caps and things.
Knickerbockers. (inaudible) Bubbles. (unintelligible)

Yeah. And Bubbles had a coat on, and always had some kind of sweater like this, you know, and the knickers, you see. But when they danced together, you know, they did excellent tap dance routines, you see. And, you know, --
What -- to what music was it that they danced?

I don't know. I can't exactly say because it might have been Liza in them times. What's the other thing? 'Blue Skies,' songs like that, you see. And they only did about two dances. Of course, the Nat Nazarra and Sons act, see, was actually, see, there's a great stars. That's in vaudeville, see. They went -- they traveled all around the world, till they became millionaires.

He would not let them discontinue their act until they became millionaires, each one of his sons, like from Cliff Nazarra to Nat Nazarra, Jr., see, and I'm telling you, this one that plays Mannix, that's one of Nazarra's sons. John Ireland, he's another one. Then, you know, Ben Gazarra, that's one of his sons, see. See, he had -- he was married twice, Nat Nazarra. He had two wives.
So and one of them had -- already had a son -- like a son, you see. It's like what they'd call a half brother, you see, or something.

Can you tell me that story about Nat Nazarra coming out on stage?

Oh, yes. That was at the Boston Conservatory of Music they used to have a show was called the Night of the Great Renowns, and this particular night Nazarra had been having Buck and Bubbles and Chuck and Chuckles off and on at the Boston Conservatory of Music. So he says that, you know, we've been having featured acts here in the Boston Conservatory of Music for quite -- many years now, and we owe our thanks to a manager who manages some of the acts, especially Buck and Bubles and an act you're going to see tonight, Chuck and Chuckles, and he said, now,

ladies and gentlemen, let's welcome the manager of Buck and Bubbles and Chuck and Chuckles, Nat Nazarro.1) And the audience stood up. Then the master of ceremonies come back onstage, and he had to actually beg the audience to let them continue the show. And then sometime later in the dressing room backstage Mr. Nazarra, he come up to Chuckles and I, he say, "You see that, cats?" He says, "That's how to do it, you see. That's what you call showmanship."
So we were very proud of him, you know. He was a wonderful man. We're going to miss him very much -- and --
What about that time when he came to the door after you hadn't seen him for a while?
(Laughter)

Oh, yeah. Yeah, well, sometime after that, a few years later I went into a rest home. I went into a home, and I had been away for about 12 and a half years. Then when I came back, I was looking up Mr. Nazarro, and -- find out where he was at. So he was up on 57th Street there at -- what's that place called? I think the Vena Park or

something, Park Venice, and -- apartments. So I finally found out what apartment he was in, and I went up to his door. I rang the bell, and he opened the door, and he was standing up in his underwear, you know.

And he says, 'Well, why didn't you call? You know, -- (Laughter) -- I said, 'I just got -- I been out of the hospital, you know, and I'm living in my aunt Brooklyn, you know, and I say I had to come over -- he told me to come and see you. I was trying to find you. I couldn't find you.'

And he says, 'How did you find me?' I said, 'Well, I went to the office where you were, and they told me that -- they gave me your address, 350 West 57th Street, apartment, so I came up.' He says, 'Well, you know, that Bubbles, he's -- you know, he's -- he hangs around some spot downtown there, you know. He's (inaudible) -- and Chuckles is getting just like him, you know. And I had been away 12 1/2 years, and that's how he was talking. Like I ain't been nowhere, you see. So anyhow I didn't see him any more after that. He passed away. of my own and --
Well, let's go on and talk -- go back to the days when you first met Buck and Bubbles. That was back in -- when you were at the Billy Pierce and Buddy Bradley Studio.
Yes, that was 1932, around February the 2nd.
Now, from the way you described it, Buck came in with Nat Nazarra, and they saw Chuck and Chuckles, and they liked the routine. Then Nazarra took you in for two years, started training you.
Yes.
He was basically training you in showmanship.
Right.
After those two years, what happened?
Well, he let us go up to Harlem, and we stayed in Mr. Bubbles' apartment with his family. And he started to training us, and --
So John Bubbles lived up in Harlem?
Yes, he had his mother and a couple of sisters, you know, like that and a niece.
And up to that point --
And his wife, yeah --
Up to that point Nazarra didn't allow you to go up to Harlem to see what was happening up there?
Never did.
So you didn't really have the influence of all the other things that were happening up in Harlem up to that point?
No, sir.
Then you go up to Harlem. And what was your first reaction of going up there? What was your feeling about the place? Well, describe what Harlem was like in those days.

Well, Harlem had a place called the Woodside Hotel. And it was very popular. That's where all the elite of Harlem mostly lived there, and in fact that's where Count Basie became famous for playing that song, 'Jumping at the Woodside.'

Well, Mr. Bubbles was very strict too, you know. He was a family man. He was only man in the family there, his -- his wife, his mother and his elder sister, and then he had a younger -- younger sister, Tiny. She lived around the corner from them. That was up at 154th Street.

And he started to training Chuckles and I, you know, and he was -- in other words, they were trying to outdo each other. Mr. Bubbles was trying to outdo Nat Nazarra, and Chuckles and I -- we were getting all these rewards of these teachings, you see, about how to perform and entertain an audience.

And at that time, see, I was supposed to be the protege of Mr. Buck. And Chuckles was supposed to be the protege of John Bubbles. But Bubbles had a way of tap dancing, an invention of his, and he had cut the tempo in half. And -- but his dancing consisted of more rhythms, better patterns of tap steps and so on, and I was trying to interest Chuckles in how to tap dance like Mr. Bubbles because I had learnt my part, see.
Mr. Buck did a chorus of dancing, but it was kind of a comical dance, you know. Nat --
What was this dance that Bubbles did? I mean can you show me that? Can you demonstrate that type of cutting and -- cutting time down, doing twice as many steps? What was that?

Well, what it was is -- during that time tap dance was an up tempo music. The music was kind of fast, you know, pieces of 'Bye-Bye Blue,' you know, and 'Liza' and 'See You in My Dreams' and pieces like that, fast tempos, you see.

So Mr. Bubbles, he cut the tempo in half and went into 4/4 time, which was -- that's a moderate tempo, rhythm, you see. And in that way, if I could be allowed to stand up here and maybe I could demonstrate some of the Bubbles sounds.
Sure.

The slapping of the thighs and --

Well, it was -- he involved the heel, the dropping of the heels, you see, into what he called cramps, cramping, like that. And like what they call a break. Like after you do a step, you would do a break, and that's where he involved this cramping.
Then he had the kick cramp, where you kick the foot
out. And that's that last part of it there where we -- you kick the foot out, and you get a cramp, see. And then you turn and you get another kind of cramp. That's the dropping of the heels, see.

And the time step, instead of it being up tempo, it was half of the tempo, you see. He called it that, rhythm tap dance, see, at that time, you see. And -- well, he was teaching me. I was asking him to teach me how to do -- it was his idea. He says, 'What's the matter with your partner? Why don't he like to dance?'

And he asked me 'Was it -- well, he's older than you. Maybe he can explain that, he said, but I tell you what. He said, 'Maybe my type of tap dancing he's not used to. He don't understand. enjoy it thataway." So Mr. Bubbles was kind of sick, you see, at that time. You know, he was just getting over a bad case of pneumonia and the loss of a wisdom tooth, you know, and he was kind of convalescing, you see. He was recovering his strength, you see.
And his mother, she inspired -- she told me how to speak to Mr. Bubbles, her son. You know, his head is still (Unintelligible) -- he'll come around, you know, which I did.

Yeah, I was there with the Sublets. His name was John W. Sublet, you see. He's --

Oh, I was going on about 17, I think, at the time.

No, no. No.

Yeah.

Oh, yes. Yes.

Well, Buck and Bubbles, you see. We

Well, the first time we went onstage with Buck and Bubbles was at the Loew's State, you see.

Well, I was going on 17, you see. But by them being adults and through the business mind of Nat Nazarra, I mean everything was legal. We'd have the proper permission, you see.

Well, that's the way I explained it because, see -- I mean he didn't seem to -- he wasn't as happy about tap dancing as I thought anyone that could do tap dancing should be, you know. And -- but it worked out like Mr. Bubbles said, you know.
