And then you tell him if he's doing it right or wrong, and then you say, "I think we better ask Mr. Bubbles, get him to show the both of us. He'll tell us if we're doing it correctly." And then he say, "Well, when I get him -- get you there, start explaining the correct way to do the steps, I take him on. I teach him how to do me", which he's supposed to really be doing, you see.

So that's what happened, but I mean J. D. still didn't learn all of Mr. Bubbles steps, which nobody in the world could Learn. Nobody, I didn't think, because I knew more of his steps than anyone, and I couldn't even do all of Mr. Bubbles' steps, you see.

hear all these feet --

You mentioned that Bubbles -- Buck and Bubbles, were the best up in Harlem at that time.
What had happened to all of the other stars? Had they either passed away, or there just weren't really that many good people up there? What was happening in Harlem?
Yeah. Well, there was a few of them there. People like Drake and Walker, Swarn and Lee, Red and Struggy -- what's that guy's name -- Orson Fry. People like that.
Where were they performing?

Well, they performed here in New York City and on the Keith Circuit, like that, you see, but what it was, Buck and Bubbles was actually stars, you see. They was box office, you see. They'd draw crowds, you see. What they called SRO, Standing Room Only, you know. They'd see Buck and Bubbles name, and that's what happened, people would flock to the theater, you see. They'd read about them, or anything like that. And they were favorites of people like Jack Dempsey, the Rothschilds, Chrysler, important people, like the mayor and the governor, Al Smith, people like that. And they were more like relations to other show people, show folk, you know, like -- men and women, like Harry Richman, the great jazz singer, and that lady -- what's her name? Belle Baker.
Let's get back now to your first performance with Buck and Bubbles, and what was that like?
Well, it was an immediate sensation. Because it was a great surprise to the public. These little

ones coming out there. They didn't know whether Buck and Bubbles had had some sons or what, you know. And by us repeating some of the jokes that Buck and Bubbles had been telling out there already that made the audience laugh, and we come out there and repeat the same jokes, and situation comedy, you know. It was an immediate sensation. That's what brought us all back together, like Nazarra, he would be back stage or out in the audience. He was watching how it worked out, because it was the two of them's idea, you see. They got so they was saying which one said the idea should be done in the act. So J.D. and I went out to do whatever they thought we should do. So we'd have to go out there and try it out with the audience, see? Different shows, see. Because we was in variety theater then, and that was variety shows. It wasn't so much vaudeville. See, the vaudeville acts was getting less and less vaudeville acts. Variety shows was becoming more popular, you see?
Well, what exactly is the difference between vaudeville and variety shows?

Well, the difference is that variety shows are -- well, they had acts, but they also would have chorus girls, you know, and production numbers going on in a variety show. Where in vaudeville they only had acts.
So basically the production value of variety shows was much more expensive, much greater.

Um-Umm. Vaudeville was more expensive, because each act considered themselves like box office, you know, headliners, stars, see. Sometimes it worked out that way, see. Will Rogers, he was in vaudeville a lot, and Walter Huston, and there was Will Mahoney, danced on a xylophone and so forth. Pat Rooney and people like that.
So you're saying that actually variety shows, even though they had greater production value, in terms of the amount of people, they were less expensive.
Yeah, they were.
Because vaudeville had all top billing.
Right.
Names. And variety shows didn't necessarily.
That's right.
It might have had one top name and the rest were fill-ins in a certain way.
That's it.
Buck and Bubbles were headliners, I take it.
Stars, yes.
So, as you began to perform more and more, you began to refine your act.
Yes.
What sort of things did you cut away from it? What sort of mistakes were you making?

Well, we weren't actually making mistakes. The idea was they loved improvement, you see, and it was either Nat Nazarra or John Bubbles thought that it would be better for us, it would be more of an improvement for to improve on there to take that away and don't do it first, do it second, and like that, whatever they had us doing. So --
Were there things that you created on your own?

Well, we had our dance, like 'Sweet Sue', and 'Broadway Melody', and 'Bugle Call Rag', you know, like those things. One time Daddy had us to doing like 'Broadway Melody', and then Buck and Bubbles' theme song, which was, 'Rhythm For Sale'. And eventually, see, they taught us how to sing the song, see, and M.C. Bubbles had sung it, and Buck and Bubbles were both of them singing it first. After they got on the stage they would sing. Bubbles would sing the verse to 'Rhythm For Sale', and then Mr. Buck was playing the piano and he joined in singing the chorus with him, and they'd sing it, you see, and people enjoyed 'Rhythm For Sale'. It was a nice melody song, you see.
How does that go?
Well, it's -- I can talk it over for you, because I'm not in too great a voice today, but I can give
you an idea how it goes. It says --
Was there tap dancing with it as well?

Yeah. Well, that's where we came in, see, because we were tap dancing "Sweet Sue". That was a melody. "Rhythm For Sale" was a special song written for Buck and Bubbles. It was a theme, like to come on stage, see?
Who wrote it?

Some fellow there. He was a freelance composer, you know. Forget his name. Nice guy, person. Well, anyhow, he specialized in that. You had a lot of music writers around Broadway then that was trying to get recognition, and he happened to be one, you know. Nazarré, Nat Nazarré knew him, you see. He got him to write this song, see. I'll explain it by words where it says. The verse of the song says, "Years ago, a certain sage said the whole world was a stage, and the colored people were the players from the start. If it's so that the colored folks, with their songs and dance and jokes, in a show must play a special part." Then it said, "Without a doubt." Then the melody begins. "All the world is rhythm mad, all the world wants rhythm bad. Colored folks are mighty glad, because they've got rhythm for sale. Everybody on this earth is in search of joy and mirth. Colored folks is rich from birth because they've got rhythm for sale. Up in Harlem they are doing swell. Nature gave them
something they can sell. Everybody on this earth is in search of joy and mirth. Colored folks are rich from birth because they've got rhythm for sale."
Isn't that something?

Yeah. That's Buck and Bubbles' theme song. So they -- eventually they taught us to sing the song and then do the "Sweet Sue" tap dance to "Rhythm For Sale". They was trying to popularize the song, you see, and that's what we did.
They would sing the song and then you would come out and tap to it.
No, we sang it.
You sang it.
They already sang it, but we come out there and they had us, instead of us doing "Sweet Sue", they had us to do -- repeat the "Rhythm For Sale" song, you see.
What sort of tap went along with it?
Well, the Short and Slim tap dance we was doing. That was the only tap dance we knew at that time, you know.
Can you tap part of it?
Well, I don't actually remember the entire routine, because my style of tap dancing changed so tremendously. Like I was taking a Ride the Horse and so forth, a few steps

that J.D. taught me. I stopped doing them, you see, because my style changed tap dancing. Actually I fell in love with the way John W. Bubbles, you know, his style of tap dancing. It was rhythm tap. It was becoming popular then, you see.
Did you feel that John Bubbles' type of tap was much more sophisticated, much --
Yes, it was.

-- more advanced, and you had already learned the other forms of tap, and up to that point they were sort of novelty sort of forms. But now you felt as if you had -- you were starting to -- your mind was starting to think in terms of more complex sort of rhythms.

Yes. See, Mr. Bubbles -- Buck and Bubbles, one time when the Jimmy Lunceford Orchestra came up to New York City, and they were all in a show one time up there, and Buck and Bubbles I would say was always stopping the show. And they'd have to do these encores. But the people loved to hear Bubbles tap dance, you know. He got a taste of what happened to me down south. They'd say, "Dance, Bubbles, Dance," and they called his name and everything. And he would say something funny about his partner had run out of music or something, and he'd say, "I'll tell you, how would you like to see me challenge this band? I'll dance against their instruments." So the audience applauds, you see. So somebody in the band would jump up and say, "How can you do

that? What instrument are you going to play?" He'd say, "I'm standing on my instrument," you see, or something like that, and make people laugh. So he says, "All right," he says, "I'll play my instrument and you repeat after me, you try to repeat after me." So he would do a step, some kind of rhythm, you know. Then one of the guys, he'd look at him, you, you. "Well, which one of you? You heard it didn't you?" And the guy would jump up with his instrument and try to play what he heard, you see. And he would choose like every member of the band would have to do something, till they get to the drums, you know. Then he'd do one, and he said, "I'm doing this here, and everybody in the band go out to do this at the same time." And he'd do another step, you see. Sure enough, they'd get up and they'd play it together, and it would sound something, you know. And it gave Mr. Lunceford an idea, I'm quite sure, because the next thing that I know of, about three weeks after that, they had a record on the juke boxes by Jimmy Lunceford and Orchestra, and it was called, "Stump the Band," and I'm quite sure that Mr. Bubbles, Buck and Bubbles inspired them to compose this song, "Stump the Band," you know. It was an instrumental, a musical number, see. But it was quite a sensation, see. And then they were always favorites. They continued to be favorites and they still are. As you know, right to this day, Mr. Bubbles is a great -- he's a great favorite with the public, you know, on television or in movies,

or whatever, you see. He's always -- he's always loved, I would say. That's really what he deserves. So I'm trying to carry on, you know. Because him not being here, you know. He hasn't been active in quite some time. I think he's convalescing, got over it. You know, I think we called him long distance on the telephone, and we talked to him, and he said something about some muscle spasm or something in one of his legs. Who knows? And eventually, I used to tell Mr. Bubbles what I was doing. And he said, 'Well, what's that? How could you do that?' And he would make me explain how I could do it. Well, he did just to make sure that I would be in time, I wouldnt get out of time, see. Like you're doing a rhythm, if you mess it up, you know, it's just like you go to write with a pencil. If you go to write a G and start to make it a J, it's not the
same thing, you see. So he was pleased.
Can you show me how he might correct you in tap? taps?
Yes.
Like do something incorrectly, and then do it, say, like he told you it should be done.

Yes.

Yeah.

Which is why you dance so great, of course.

You didn't stand still.
No.
Always progressing.
Yes.
Which is why it sounds so --

Yes. Yes, he did. He invented that. He invented that style of tap dancing.
Which requires a lot of --
Yeah.
-- great technique.

That's the point, I think, we were trying to get over. It's that much more progressive, because we're coming down from just using the ball of the foot to using the whole of the foot.
Yeah.
Adding heels.
Uh-huh.
Which people even now find very difficult, to use heel and toe beats.
Yes.
It's extremely progressive.

It gives out a different sound?
Yeah. The stomping of the heel -- the heel is more like what they call the foot drum to a tap dancer, you see. But he was using both of the heels. Therefore that caused what he called a cramp.

Speaking of the cramp, Chuck, what would you say -- I mean it would take a student who would really have to be technically on top or what have you, to be able to do those cramp rolls and make them sound so -- look so easy, but we know it's not easy. How many years did that -- you know, did it take you tap dancing before you developed that style to be able to handle those cramps like that, like sort of falling off a log, for want of another expression?

Well, we were with the Buck and Bubbles act for four and a half years. And we were never allowed to be away from Mr. Bubbles -- Nat Nazarrq. We didn't stay with Mr. Buck because Mr. Buck had just his wife, you see. And three of those years, during three of those years, Mr. Bubbles, he trained Chuckles and I in tap dancing, what he called putting us through the paces. And he would make Chuckles and I dance a series of tempos, just to shape us up and make us stronger, because we were still growing lads, you see. And he

used to take us around to the Rockland Palace, and he took us to a place on St. Nicholas Avenue called the Hotcha Club, and he took us to the Renaissance Ballroom, you know, and of course these was all wooden floors, and that's to keep us from getting anything like a hardening of the arteries. Most dancers used to be very afraid of getting hardening of the arteries. I don't see why, because they was -- in that kind of activity, I don't see why they could be getting any hardening of the arteries, because it consisted all -- the entire ability of tap dancing is action, see, it's activity. But he explained that to dance on concrete and artificial composition floors and things like that, that it was dangerous to the arteries, because you could get hardening of the arteries, or you would get what they called the charley horse. You know, like swimmers get it. He's swimming in the water and he get's --
In the calves.

Yeah. In the muscles, you see. And then, as I said, we were still growing lads, and that's what he did. And all during these times I was very inquisitive, you see, because whenever I wanted anything explained to me that I thought wasn't an actual fact, I would ask my aunt, Edna May Sanders, 'Am I doing it right?' or 'Am I correct?' or 'Is it a good idea to do it this or that way?' you know. So I had -- actually I had three -- well, four teachers, I mean

to myself they were teachers, because I would ask Tiger Flowers questions about, like rhythms, you know, and he would always say, "Well, I'm the student and you're teacher." He couldn't explain the rhythms to me, the way that Mr. Bubbles did, or either J.D., Chuckles.

(Unintelligible) the kick cramp was much richer than the walking cramp, which is absolutely true. Because that is so. The walking cramp is on one foot, and the kicking cramp is two, on two feet. And that's what happened. So I was in the midst of it all, and I was trying to teach myself different ways of doing a tap step more than one way. So I had a little tour that I used to go on and I wandered as far down as what they called the Hoofer's Club. That was down there by the Lafayette Theater, at 131st and 7th Avenue. Now, 7th Avenue was known as the main stem at that time, and eventually Duke Ellington composed a song, a jazz song, called "Main Stem". I think I have the record. And Mr. Bubbles was saying that that was one of his favorite pieces of music. So one time we had the radio on, in Mr. Bubbles' house, and this piece came over the radio, "Main Stem", and the Duke Ellington Orchestra, you see. And it was gorgeous jazz music, you know, this "Main Stem", and if anyone ever achieved a tap dance to this,
I think they would reach the heights of stardom, because it's really brilliant.
(Recording Interruption)

Yeah, I would go on this tour, and I wandered as far down as the Hoofer's Club. I didn't know there was a Hoofer's Club at that time. I didn't know, and I had never seen much of Harlem, but 154th Street and up there around the Polo Grounds, you see, so I wandered down there and I found out that that's where there was some kind of dancers, tap dancers. They had a fraternity from the Hoofer's Club, and they had some kind of initiation going on. Where you would have to -- there was a tree called the Tree of Hope, and you wasn't allowed to stand under this tree unless you could dance by some kind of melody. And it wasn't considered a dance, a tap dance, unless you could dance -- tap dance -- 32 bars, which was a melody, of any song.
Chuck, I'd like you to demonstrate exactly what that is. Can you do that right now? Would you like to stand up, or can you do it sitting?
Yeah, I'd rather stand up.
Okay.
(Recording interruption)

Well, here I am, about to demonstrate 32 bars of tap dancing, which is a melody, and that was the fraternity's initiation of the tap dancers who went in and were allowed to touch the Tree of Hope and go down into the Hoofer's Club. So I'll now demonstrate 32 bars of tap dancing.
(Tap dancing.)
See? That was 32 bars of tap dancing.

I can't find any words to tell you how sharp that is. I mean it's so much going on in your feet. I saw the cramps and all the different steps. I could practically see the history of tap dancing, just watching you in those 32 bars. How did it look to you, George?
It was really fantastic.

That was a Charleston beat you finished up on, right? Great. So of course because of that, naturally they took you in. You became a member immediately at the Hoofer's Club. They opened the doors for you immediately and dragged you in.
(Recording interruption)

See, now that's the initiation, like life. The Hoofer's Club's life, their fraternity, that was their life. And here comes a new recruit. They wouldn't allow you to touch the Tree of Hope unless you could tap dance by one chorus which is 32 bars of any music or song you preferred. And once you started you got to go around, you got to tap dance around four blocks. You tap danced from 7th Avenue, in front of the Hoofer's Club, down 131st Street to Lenox Avenue, then up Lenox Avenue to 132nd Street, and then up 132nd Street, Then, if you didn't miss any taps, they allowed you to touch the Tree of Hope. And once you'd been allowed to Touch the Tree of Hope,
the time of your life begins, tap dancing.
So tell me a little bit about that Hoofer's Club. What was it like? What was the layout?

Well, it was like a very rich, luxurious nightclub, what they call like a cabaret. But everything in there was maybe four or five times as much as any other rich nightclub, see? They had palm trees. They had would-be banana trees. Frangipani trees. And bamboo fences. And then they had what they called a vine chair. This chair was like a throne. It was made out of all vines. Wild vines, (unintelligible) vines, raw vines, you know. And they made up this throne. So whoever got to be like the leader of the tap dancers in the Hoofer's Club fraternity, they were considered, he's the king. Tap dancing jazz.
But tell me a little bit about the guy that owned the Hoofer's Club and the way it was laid out. There was a front room and there was a back room for the dancers. What was in the front room?

Oh, yes. That was Mr. Dudley, his name was. John Dudley, I think. He used to be a first violinist. And Mr. Frank Schiff was the Lafayette Theater there. Until he reached his retirement, which was -- they were in the house orchestra, see? He was. First violinist. And when his retirement came he had some savings, so he bought this Hotcha Club, it used to be, an ex-nightclub. And by the tap dancers coming

down there, he used to adopt these tap dancers, the ones that were allowed to get into the Hoofer's Club fraternity. And he renamed the place in honor of the tap dancers, the Hoofer's Club. It really was a recreation place, you know, for people to come and relax and have lunches and dinners and so on, you know. They had a gorgeous kitchen there. See, it was a circular kitchen, so you had number one chef, number two chef, and so on, on down the road, see? And they fixed everything. Whatever you wanted, any way in the world, them chefs could get it off the stove, see? And a lot of us tap dancers used to go down in there, at least when they accepted me and I was of age, you see. That was the proof of my age, by being a member of the Hoofer's Club, which I was honorary, see? So what I did was right away I got to be the one that sat in the vine chair. (Laughter). You see? And so I did prosper. It was the time of my life. We never looked back after that, my partner and I. One of us at least, you know, if a tap dancing act whether there's one, two, or a trio or a quartet or a quintet, you know, whatever, if one of the members of the act was in the fraternity of the Hoofer's Club, his whole act was considered, you know, as members.

And tell me a little bit about the front part of the Hoofer's Club. What was there? It was two rooms, right? What would happen when you walked down the steps? There was an awning outside, and you'd walk down the steps and

You would enter into like a village, which was like in the jungles, way deep in the jungles, exactly like the replica of a little village way in the midst of Africa, the darkest of Africa, you see. And they used to have like these tom-toms, these African drums, hanging from the ceilings, you see. And they had lights in them, you see. So, see, because the Hotcha Club, they was trying to overtake, like, the Cotton Club. See, the Cotton Club was considered the tops of all niteries here in New York City at that time. And the people that opened the Hotcha Club, I think they was the radio people, you know. They used to broadcast from the Cotton Club, and I think they got the idea by them broadcasting from the Cotton Club, why shouldn't they own a nightclub of their own, you know. And so that's what happened. But no-one ever knew for sure.
Well, weren't there billiard tables, also?

Yes. They had sporting rooms in there. They had that. They had game rooms which they called them, and yeah, fountains, you know, ice cream parlors and like that, you see. All that's in the nightclub. They called it the Hotcha Club, you see.
Then in the back, the back room.
Yeah. That was a ballroom.
And that was eventually what became the Hoofers' Club.
That was it.
So you'd walk in there and there was a big dance floor.

Yeah. Well, after you'd get through the village -- if you don't go in the game room, you see, right away you can go -- the next step is into the -- where the bandstands are, see? Because they had bandstands. They had about three bands going in there.
In the ballroom?
Yeah. In the Hotcha Club, it was called maybe.
Well, when was the Hoofers' Club first originated? Was it after the Hotcha Club, or were both of them going on at the same time?

No. That was after Mr. Dudley -- I was talking about his retirement from the Lafayette Theater. He had saved up some money, and this Hotcha Club was out then, it was closed, you know. It was up for lease. And he took the lease on it and eventually paid for it, you see. But he renamed it after tap dancers, which he always admired in the shows at the Lafayette as he played throughout the years. That way he kept in touch with most of his great friends, which was our performers.
So when the Hotcha Club changed into

Yeah, yeah. Well, that's in the lobby. That's when you first come in, you see, the village. Like I say, palm trees, would be banana trees, frangipani trees, the tom-toms hanging from like the sky with lights in it, you see. That's the village. That's the entrance to the original Hotcha Club.
And then you'd enter into the game room.
Then you would enter into the game room. Yes.
Which had billiard tables and --
Yes. They had billiard tables, card tables --
It was a gambling casino in a certain way.
Yeah. Roulette wheels.
And then, if you wanted to go into the back, that's where you'd enter into what was known then as the Hoofer's Club.
Yeah. That was the Hoofer's Club.
Which was a big ballroom?
Oh, yes. It was a gorgeous room.
I've heard stories that he had to
change the floor often because the dancers were so hard on the floor he kept having to change it.

(Laughter) Yes. The tap dancers. They were busy creating works, you see, like melodies, routines in tap dancing. See? Because the more versatile you were in those days, the more employment you would acquire, see?
So, what sort of things were happening at the Hoofer's Club?

Oh, well, I mean they eventually acquired Dancing Dodson. That's where he come from. He was acquired from there. He went on to be like -- he was considered like the Chocolate Harry Richman, see. He was a jazz singer and dancer. He was a dancer -- the popular dance in those times was the Strut, you know, what you called showing your figure, you know, your build, your masculinity, or whatever, you know, and that's what he -- he was one of the best at the Hoofer's Club, and then there was King Rastus. He was turned out from there. Quite a few others. Ah, yeah, and one, he could do 103 different wings. That was Willie Green. He was turned out from the Hoofer's Club fraternity. He went on to great heights. And then there was Step'n'Fetchit. Of course you know about Step'n'Fetchit. He's an old man considered a legend now. And he's one of Muhammad Ali's favorite personalities, you see. In fact he's a favorite personality of all the world, you know, in his day. And I think his day is here
again, you see.
Tell me a little bit about King Rastus Brown at the Hoofer's Club. What was he like in the Hoofer's Club?
Well, King Rastus Brown introduced what they called buck dance, see. He was the originator of that, buck dance. You see?
What is a buck dance?

Well, now, I could get up and show you a demonstration and explain it also. As a tap dancer would be dancing, when he gets to the improvisation of the melody or song, there was what was known as a break, and he had in the buck dance, introducing this break, and that's where you would see the buck. It's like a deer, like a running deer. He runs so much, and then he would jump, you know, about three or four jumps and leaps like that. Well, each time this occurs in the buck dance, that's what he named it after. He named it buck dance because of that character in the dance.
It would be nice if you could show me that. Shall we do it?
Sure, certainly.
(Mr. Green tap dancing.)
Did you see the bucks? I made about $15.00. (Laughter). Yeah, well that's the authentic buck dance, see, and King Rastus Brown, that's what he introduced
from the Hoofers Club fraternity.
(Recording interruption)
Chuck, is that used now, the way you were doing the buck dance? Do you use that now?
Yes. Twice.
Do you use it exactly as you've used it there, or have you changed it, or --
Well, I've given it what you call a more --
Embellished on it?
More equipment, yes. More installation in it. All the great, great dancers, tap dancers, featured a time step somewhere in their tap dance.
Because you say that was Dancing Dodson.
No. That was King Rastus Brown.
Oh, I beg your pardon. I beg your pardon. Yes. But he does go -- he goes quite a way back, King Rastus.
King Rastus Brown does, yes, he goes quite a ways back.
So you say you do utilize that same buck dance in your dancing today. That's just a part of it.
Right. Every tap dancer, somewhere in their tap dance is the buck dance.
Uh-huh. It's a common dance used.

It's considered, you know, greatly artistic. That's why the -- what you call clogging, you know, waltz clogging, tap dance, that's how that was moved out, because of buck dancing, you see. Buck dancing became a favorite with other tap dancers. So they discontinued these dances like the strut, see, and clogging.
I would imagine it does, because it's very musical, and I see you were using your heels.
Yes.
Which most dancers find that difficult to do, even today.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, everytime he had something, he would say (Unintelligible). In buck dancing you touch the heel to begin what was known as the change, which is a break. After each step, the tap dancer demonstrated a tap break, and his tap, instead of using like the whole -- the ball of the foot or, you know, the toe and the heel of the foot, he would just use the heels. That was like a push. You call that pushing off, because he got the buck, to start the buck, like the jump or the leap, see, and it's like a buck, like in a rodeo, when the horse bucks, you see.
Would you say that most of the people that became members of the Hoofer's Club were in general sort of pioneer in their own way? They have contributed at least one step or one style to a step?

That's it, exactly, yes. They started a new fashion, see? It was like being in -- where they make automobiles, see. Air vehicles, you see, airplanes, as they would say. See, they was making these different engines, you see. That's what was happening to tap dancing, you see.
Creating a different pattern.
Oh, yes.
These were the things that made you sort of an honorary member.
Yeah.

Well, what other dancers were there that created particular steps that were innovative for those times? I know you mentioned Tip, Tap and Toe, as the kings -- certain kings of the Hooper's Club at one time.
(Recording interruption)

Well, there was the Berry Brothers. Yes, and the Five Hotshots. And of course, naturally, Buddy Bradley. See, he became the great teacher of tap dancing, and was known as the rhythm dancer. See? Let me see. Where was Buddy Bradley originally from? Wasn't he from Washington, D.C.?
Pennsylvania.
Oh, yes. Pennsylvania. Yes.
The Hotshots. Who were the Hotshots?
Well, they was a pioneer tap dance team that was considered geniuses, see, by many, because they were

all some similar to Eddie Rector, the tap dancer, who was known as the Gentleman of the Evening. They wore these high hat and tails. Oh, they worked from one year throughout the other year, through the next year. I mean, there was plentiful work for them, because there was five of them. And they became popular very easily from developing their dances at the Hoofers Club.
But what exactly did they do? They all came out in top hats and tails. They were a class act, I take it.

Yes. They were like -- well, it's like day school and night school, see. They was the tops, you see. You couldn't get no classier than high hat and tails at that time. That was considered the most fashionable attire. I mean the most immaculate male or men's clothes that there could be. That was the top of the wardrobe.
Was it unusual for blacks to be wearing those clothes?

Well, in a way they were, because the blackface -- the minstrels had popularized the high hat and tails, because they was all considered doctors, you see. Remember minstrel shows, they had these -- they called themselves medicine shows, and they -- with the minstrels, you see. And they -- I think they introduced the high hat and tails to the public, so far as being in shows or on stage or in
entertainment. See? Otherwise, a man -- it was considered in every day wear, you see, but the very rich, they wore them kind of clothes, in different parts of the day.
But it wasn't -- for the black community it wasn't common to see people in high hat and tails, was it?
Only on special occasions like great holidays or something, parties, birthday parties and marriages and so forth, like that.
Well, were the Hotshots the first group, black group, to wear high hats and tails, or were there other groups prior to that?

Oh, there were plentiful prior to them. But it was outstanding on them, you see, because the blacking of the face, what they called the blackface comedians, they had went out of fashion, see, as they come along.
This was what time?

Well, it was early in -- I'm saying right after -- it was right after -- I think this was during -- after the Depression, you see. What they called after the '29 crash, right, the stock market crash in 1929, right? And after that I think our President made some -- spoke to the nation about how to overcome the Depression, not to let the Depression get the better of them and stop jumping out of windows and committing suicide, because they was going to

introduce Prohibition. Things became plentiful then when they introduced, bringing in the Prohibition, you see. They was going to legalize liquors and things, you see. And that made the high hat and tails very famous too, because people used to go out, you know, after the daytime, at night you know, where they could get a little kissey, see? And that's how they would dress. They would wear these high hat and tails, you know, and wherever they go.
Was this particularly up in Harlem that you're referring to, where people would go out?

Oh, yes. Especially in Harlem, yes. See, they had -- see, those places were -- well, it was kind of mysterious, because Harlem was famous in those days for being a happy place. There was always a lot of laughter going on. And there were some great people up there, you know, in Harlem, you know. Sometimes there was Paul Robeson. You know he was great. And there was Bert Williams. He was great, you see.

Let me -- as long as you got onto Bert Williams, I'm particularly taking an interest in him because of his sense of humor, his unique sense of humor. And if there's any routines that you remember of him, I think that that would be very interesting for you to tell. (Recording interruption) What sort of -- if you don't remember the particular routines, what were the names of some of the songs he used to do?
Well, he did something -- he did something about a hole card. Ace up the sleeves. He did something about, 'Officer, can you show me how to cross to the other side of the street?'

The Desserts?

Oh, yeah.
Well, did he add a little routine to that? Did he do different types of walk? This is how you walk when you're happy, this is how you walk when you're sad?
Yes. Yes.
What was the nature of his routine?
Yes, that was him. That's his work. That's exactly the way.
Character walks.
Yes. He did do -- how he would walk if he couldn't see his best girl, and how he would walk when he finally did see her. Then how he'd walk after he had done seen her, you see.
What other kinds of things would he do in his routine?

Well, he had a way of being light on his feet, you see, because he looked to be the size of about, I'd say a little over 300 pounds. And he was very tall, see. and Foster. But he was famous before then, you see. But he was one of the Hoofer's Club's members, you see.

He worked in and out of blackface. He wore the high hat and tails. But he was greatly known for his tap dancing. His tap dancing was loved mostly. But he was a great comedian, also.

No, no. They was just clever tap dancers.
Eccentric.
Clever.

Well, it's -- they had to demonstrate some kind of -- type of work, type of routine, you see.
Would you say an originality?
Yes. That's it. Yes. A new appearance. Like a That's the degree.

Oh, yeah. A senior, you see. He had been

on the throne. See, that's really what made me wander down on this tour, there. Yes.

Yes.

But I was travelling a lot then, you know, with the new
Chuck and Chuckles, see.
With Buck and Bubbles at that time.
Yeah.
This was at the height of your performance with Buck and Bubbles, when you were about 18?
Yeah. Yeah. I had become 18, you know.

from Chuck and Chuckles?

How did that song go?
Well, it was something. All dressed up, high hat and everything. All dressed up, looking good and (unintelligible). he can sing. (Singing), "There he goes. Here am I, breaking in a pair of shoes."
Can you sing it, Chuck?

No, sir. Looley, here, I sings, you know, but I don't sing without an instrument. And as you know, well you do have a radio somewhere. Well, I'll get a song to sing for you. Like a poet would explain in a poem, you see. It was like that.

(Laughter)
Well, I never did -- when was it? I
You were dancing while you were singing?

See, once they pass, you see these people died, you see. I try to discontinue remembering some of the things that we were mostly attached to, you see. Because I was kind of hurt when they passed.
