Yes, there was Roland Holden. He used to -- that was one of Buddy Bradley's students. And I tell you, I think Mr. Bradley called him 'hookey player', see, because he was a cute little man, and he was a great friend, you know. We were good buddies, you see.
How did he inspire you, Roland Holden?

Well, he used to dance to this famous melody. All the pianists used to like to play this. They called it "Nola", or, "Doll Dance" (singing), or "Kitten on the Keys". It's like a doll dancing, you see. And he had a way of -- he wore these spats and patent leather shoes, you know, and he was in the high hat and tails, you see. Or either he'd talk, you know. But his tap dancing, I thought, I thought it was splendid to watch and listen to, and I liked it.
What was it that really took your eye and your ear?

It was one of the steps that he got from his class, from his dancing class, you see, with the Buddy Bradley, you know, lessons. And when he just got that one step, you know, and he built a tap routine around it and chose this piece, the "Doll Dance".
What do you think the difference was with that step? Was it the way it was paced or the style of it?
Yes. It was very loving, you see. It was just like being caressed by a soft breeze, you know. Of course you would like to see it, you would like to hear it over and over again, you see.
Can you demonstrate that step?
(Laughter) Yeah, I always can demonstrate that one. (Tap dancing.) (Nierenberg interrupts the dancing)
Could you do a little bit more?
All right.
It's so pretty. It really is pretty. Do you agree, George, it's really pretty?
(Tap dancing.)
Is that up the sleeve?
It certainly is. As I said, Chuck, I think that was very pretty. Do I detect, after you finished the Buddy Bradley step, some Bill Robinson?
Always.
Tagged on the end? A tag doggy eight?
Always.
You know there's That is a distinct -- there's a distinct difference with anybody who studied it.
Yes. Well, you know, he was the Mayor of Harlem, you see, and he was a great champion of the tap dancing, because he introduced the tap dancing from the Hoofer's Club. He was in the fraternity.
Bill Bojangles.

Yes. And we were trying to keep one of the songs from the Hoofer's Club fraternity which was introduced by, written especially for, Bill Bojangles Robinson, about tap dancing and how, when he was acquiring his idea of calling the tap dancing tap dancing, and in other words, I'm doing his degree, of the Depression at that time.
This was the year -- early '30s?
Early '30s. That was the young Bill Bojangles Robinson.
But the first step was Buddy Bradley, the pretty step.
Yes.
I can understand your being very interested, because that is a pretty step if that was done like that then.
Yes. Oh, Roland -- well, I'd say it like Mr. Buddy Bradley said it --
Because there's a distinct difference in that first step and the second step, which was obviously Bill Bojangles.
Yeah. Yeah.
So Roland Holden really made his success on that one great step.
He built a routine around it.
I don't blame him.
Yes.
It's very pretty step.
Well, would you say that most tap dancers were limited in their scope as dancers? They only had one particular routine, and they'd just do it over and over and really didn't expand?

No. They were required to do a certain amount of minutes, which is 5-1/2 minutes. They would have to have a dance routine, or tap dance appearance, as it was known then. That approximated 5-1/2 minutes of program, see. So there was all kinds of tap dancing. There was what they called the Freddie James tap dancing. That was known as close rhythm, you see. Just like when you're closing an envelope on a letter, or something like that.
I'm not sure I know what you mean. Could you explain that a little bit further?

Yeah, well, close rhythm was -- you would make the taps in triplets instead of singles our couples. You see? It was almost a nerve tap, see, and it was as rapid as a nerve tap. But it was more supple, more nimble, and more -- what is it called there? Oh, the word is ambidextrous, I think.
Well, a nerve tap is what, exactly?
Well, that's tapping with one toe. In other words, it was a hand getter, it would cause applause.
But close rhythm was different from nerve tap.
Yeah. That was like instead of using one foot you'd use two feet.
I'd love to see that.
Triplets, yeah, we called it.
Can you do that for us?
Sure, I could do some of it.
(Mr. Green tap dancing.)
That was great. Can you show us some nerve tapping?
(Mr. Green tap dancing.)
Wow. That, I would say, is real jazz tap dancing. Well, that's my idea of jazz tap.
It better be.
I think even George could see the difference in the different styles of the different dances that you've done. Did you George?
Well, what exactly is -- explain to me the difference. What is it that you're doing that makes it more innovative than the other steps?

Well, it's because if you separate the nerve tap and put it on two feet instead of one, which is single and double, see, you make two beats with any foot, that was considered tap dancing, you see. So the nerve -- the separation, the difference between the two is that one -- the nerve tap is actually like standing on one foot and shaking one foot, you know, and like trembling, you see? It's very religious, you see, because it was a form of happy -- what they call happy, happy. I don't intend to be -- no disrespects, I'll say, but in churches, sometimes.
This seemed to me to be a heavy mix. I notice cramp rolls and sort of like a paddling roll, a mixture of lots of things that you have to be technically superb to do.

Yes. Well, the paddling and roll always be a superb tap dance, because right now it's supposed to be the juvenile of tap dancing, it's the newest work of tap dancing, you see. If At the Hoofer's Club, it was still in being, this would be considered a degree from the Hoofer's Club fraternity, for making a good picture. (recording interruption)

I just said to you, Chuck, that that looked to me like cramps and paddling rolls and things. Was that a little bit before the paddling roll really became the paddling roll and the cramp? So, let me see, now, I would say that Freddie James probably inspired whoever it was, and that would be interesting to know who did, who was the first person who did bring about the paddling roll and the cramp? Because you say that wasn't quite the paddling roll and it wasn't quite a cramp. So it's obviously whoever were the first people to do that, they were inspired by Freddie James. Could you --

Yeah. Well, there were three of them that were inspired by Freddie James, but the original paddling roll came from a tap dancer known as Billy Adams and Ground Hog, see, and then there was Billy Yates and Baby Lawrence.
He was the modernistic debonair, what you would call. I called him the youngest pioneer that came into being of tap dancing, and --
Baby Lawrence.

Yes. The late, great Baby Lawrence. I called him Bravery, because he feared no sounds. And he always inspired all the other tap dancers. In fact, he was the cause of a brotherhood of tap dancers which occurred in New York's Jazz Museum here.
This is tape number 11 of Chuck Green.

Well, I was answering a question about the paddling roll, which is the newest style of tap dancing that's been introduced, and at the Hoofer's Club was still in existence, where it would be considered a new work and a new degree at the Hoofer's Club fraternity.
(Recording interruption)
Well, let me redirect the conversation a little bit, because we're getting a little bit more towards more modern type jazz and tap dancing.
Yeah.

I'd like to go back a bit to the era of the Hoofer's Club and the type of tap that was being done then. You had mentioned Roland Holland and you had mentioned Bill Robinson. Now let's get into Bill Robinson.

Well, he was a sport. He was a very happy personality, a great personality. He was a track star too, and his work, which was tap dancing, became like what you would call a relay runner on a track, passing the stick and so on, steeplechasing or whatever, and he could do 26 different tap dance dances. So he got discovered by some millionaire, happened to see him. He used to go around and from one theater amateur contest to the other theater's amateur contest, so that way he would get a chance to do about four shows a day, you see? And if he didn't win one amateur contest, he'd probably win the other one, you see? As long as he'd at least win one or two, you see. And that's how he developed his tap dancing, because he was applying new degrees to the art itself. See, they had to make book on the history of the tap dancers. That was Mr. Dudley, the owner of the Hoofer's Club, that's what he did, because they were his favorite performers, the tap dancers. And that's really why Mr. Buddy Bradley and Mr. Dudley was kind of -- they were very well acquainted and they had been co-workers, see. And --
But Bill Robinson, I've heard stories about him, he used to carry around a gun with him.
Yes. That was from the Police Department. The Police Commissioner gave him a gold plated 38 special. It

had a pearl handle. And he had two of them. He had the set, you see. And he was so proud of them. He would always carry one along with him, and he would come along to the gaming rooms of the Hoofeer's Club, see, because finally he got another place around the corner for musicians, and he separated the tap dancers from the musicians, see. And he used to come around the gaming rooms with this pearl handled -- at least one of them -- gold plated pistol. But he would have the bullets out of the pistol. And he used to bluff some of the sports, you see. They were playing different recreation in there, like shooting pool, or billiards or something, you know, or whatever. They'd make wagers on things, like who would buy the supper or who would treat the house or who would go to buy the refreshments, whatever. Who'd go pay the landlord the rent. Or anything to cause joy, happiness. And he eventually became the Mayor of Harlem, on account of his ways, his actions, and voluntary works, the charity works that he did. And that way he got a chance to expose tap dancing more and more, until eventually everyone had agreed that tap dancing was tap dancing, you see?
You mentioned before that he would bluff people with his gun. Can you tell me any stories like that?
Well, it was just like, say for instance he'd be playing heads or tails, like flipping a coin. And he'd

flip a gold coin, like a $20.00 what do you call it -- gold piece. He'd flip that, you see. And there'd be two of them flipped, and he'd say, "Heads or tails. Whoever guesses gets," you see. And if he would choose tails and it would come up heads. He would pull out his gold pistol and make it whatever he chose, you see, because I mean his opponent didn't know whether the pistol was, you know, loaded or unloaded, you see. And he'd say, "Gets," you see, instead of saying heads or tails. They have agreed that that's what they're going to flip the $20.00 gold piece. Well, they had so many different kinds of gold pieces there, because they was trying to make people forget about the depression. And he was spreading happiness at this time and popularizing tap dancing.
Do you think he had the greatest influence?

Yes. Definitely. Yeah, he had the greatest influence, he and John Bubbles, you see, of Buck and Bubbles. See, because Jack Wiggins was not -- I think he was unknown up here at that time. He used to travel on the TOBA, and that was mostly in the south, you know. And therefore, Bill Bojangles Robinson was making tap dancing recognizable when people would -- when they'd speak of tap dancing, they'd speak of it like they speak of ballet, you see. Because there was a lot of different works in tap dancing, see? You had what they called the unison tap. They had precision tap

dancing. They had novelty tap dancing, you see. And they had trick tap dancing. His tap dancing consisted of steps. And that was tap dancing. Because he would always say -- he had a routine where he would say, "Number one tap step." And when he would demonstrate the number one tap step. But it was fascinating. As I say, they all would do some kind of buck. See? And he had a way of doing the time step, and he called that number one step, you see?
Was his way of doing the time step different from other dancers' ways of doing the time step?
Yes.
What would he do, he'd go up on his toes more?

Yes. Yes. He was very masculine, see. He was manly about it. He Looked So refreshing, you know. Just like watching big drops of rain coming down, he was so even. Well, he really was ambidextrous. Anything that he could do on one foot, he could do on the other. Both feet he could do. Then he could do some of the steps with both feet at the same time, and that's how this dance, this tap dance he called number one step, number two step, number three step, number four step, number five step, and that's the tap dance routine, see?
Can you do some of that Bill Robinson stuff?
Yeah, well I can do what he taught me.
Okay.
(Mr. Green tap dancing.)
Great.
I'd like to hear that one again. (Recording interruption)

Super. Super. Well, Chuck, one would think that actually was Bill Bojangles, because it's so perfect. Your footwork is so perfect. I've seen him many times, fortunately, on the movies, and I mean your feet are exactly like his.

Yes. Well, he would only allow the best you could do. If he taught you any tap step. And he never would teach you an entire tap dance routine. He would teach you how to begin to tap dancing, see? And you would have to either buy a ticket or wait till he'd bring some tickets around the Tree of Hope, or you could go into the lobby of the theater or wherever he was playing in New York City at that time, and see him tap dance. And try to learn yourself some of the tap steps.
He must be very pleased with you. The step that you do where you draw your toes back and you draw it back and hit the toe --
Yeah. He called that a lower. That was getting the straw first for the hula. Haloha.
That's a Bojangles original?

Yes, that is. And he did it circularly. That's why you hear the moving. It's supposed to be -- convey the sound of like the propellors going off or the ship putting on brakes, you see. You hear the turbulence.
I know you're very fond of that step and you carry it with you wherever you go.
Yes.
Because we see you use it -- you still use that up to today, here and there.
Yeah, well --
Well, what does that step do for you as a performer? Like how do you feel when you're doing it? Why do you add it in at certain moments?

Well, because the most important sound in tap dancing is the moving. If you're tap dancing and you begin to moving as you're tap dancing, that's considered travelling. And as I was saying, that's one of his first routines. See, he numbered each one of his tap dances, like one, two, three, four, up to 26. Because musically, in those times, those days, the tap dancer was allowed two bars of music introduction. And then a 24 bar chorus of music was considered one chorus, instead of 32 bars. Because, as I said before, they were working on the Depression, see, so they tried to do the best -- most of the best right away, abruptly, see, that's to keep the
nation, the people, from getting into a lull again, or starting to getting disastrous thoughts about their life.
And of course, tap dancing being the music of the feet, a step like that, the one where you make that sound where you draw your foot back and hit your toe, this is just another musical tone or sound.
Yes.
That adds to all the pretty sounds that we do make with the feet.
Yes.
Well, what music was that type of dancing performed to?
It was performed to like jazz, the early jazz, what they call.
What composers?

Oh, well, as I say, they had -- I like to say Duke Ellington, because I thought he was the greatest. But there was Sissle and Blake. One was a great singer and band leader and one was a great pianist, musician. He is a professor of music.
Well, that dance that you just did then, what music went with that?
Well, he called it the Pretty Foot, see, because it represented one step that he favored, and he favored the step because it was moving, see. He's walking as

he's moving, see. And he'd be telling jokes as he'd be walking. He'd be speaking to someone or welcoming a new customer that's coming in, arriving in the theater, or coming down the aisle, or being seated, or whatever. And that's why he called it the Pretty Foot, because if he'd see some new customers coming in, he'd know that his salary would be guaranteed. Yeah, he was a -- well, he got to be like a spirit in Harlem. He and Buck and Bubbles and people like Bert Williams, you see, and Paul Robeson, they were like spirits.
Bill Robinson seemed to be a real character.
Yes.
What kind of --
A great personality he was.
What kind of things would he do?

Well, he would say words, you know, a way of talking. He would introduce new plays, like in sports. Like who could throw the darts. You know. Who could balance the cards or make a card house, and so forth. Or who could play dice, dominoes, galloping dominoes. That was a pastime.
What's galloping dominoes?
Well, it's some bones, square bones, and they've got numbers on them, like from one to six. And you

really can go up, and as a pair they would go from one to twelve -- two to twelve, like that. And you had to shake them in your hand like a fist, and then open your hand and they would roll out, and they would gallop and stop on some kind of number. And whatever number they'd stop on, the tap dancer would have to do that many steps. Tap steps. So he would always try to stop on eight, because that was equal to 24 bars of music, see. So if he'd make eight, that's his point, he has to make eight again. So eight would be 16. And that way, that's when they brought in the 32 bars of music, see. Because of his -- well, we called it sports. He was, like I say, a spirit. He was a great inspiration at that time to the people that was going along in the Depression. Things wasn't as rich as they were, but they was sending each other a thought.
It's interesting that you should mention the galloping dominoes, him playing with numbers, because you told me a very similar story about you and he playing pool on his 22nd birthday.
Yeah.
Why don't you tell me that story?
Well, that's it. I mean, he would introduce these plays which was known as a game. But I mean he made his living at it at the same time, by -- of course that was his job, was tap dancing, see, and --
Tell me about the story you told me.

Well, once upon a time, as time came on or came by or passed, he eventually got into moving pictures with Shirley Temple, the child actress star. He used to teach her. He used to do choreography for him and her. And he called it terpsichore, he said, and he would make up these dance routines, tap dances, you know, like the adult and the child tap dances, and Shirley Temple and Bill Bojangles Robinson. Like they did the melody, "Bojangles of Harlem", and that went, (Singing), "Old Bojangles of Harlem," they were saving a plantation while they sang and tap danced, that they introduced in this movie. I think it was the "Little Colonel", I think it was called. Eventually he came on what you call a personal appearance tour at the time, and Chuck and Chuckles was with the Don Redmond Orchestra and show, and that was Mr. Glen Peg Leg Bates and Dan Jenkins, Chuck and Chuckles, Louise McCarroll, Sonny Woods, and starring Bill Bojangles Robinson, the World's Chamption Tap Dancer. We were in Boston, Massachusetts, at the RKO Palace, and it was during the week of his birthday. Now, as it had been quite some years since I had saw Mr. Bojangles, Bill Bojangles Robinson, see, but I had got into -- I knew him from the Rhythm Club. As I say, the gaming room in the Hoofer's Club. And one night there Mr. Don Redmond used to teach a friend of mine, a great tap dancer pioneer, was

Baby Lawrence, and he used to take us to the gaming room, and he was teaching us how to shoot pool, how to play position with the cue ball. In other words, how to run the largest amount of balls. You have to put them in the pockets. And they were considered as points. Well, Mr. Bill Bojangles Robinson, he would like to wager, you see, so he figured that Mr. Don Redmond, being a band leader, the orchestra leader, and famous, with the (Unintelligible), the jazz giants, you see, he would make a wager. He would give odds. He said he -- "How many points do you want?" he'd say. "I'll allow you 25 points and I'll play you and whatever partner you would choose 500 points, see? So naturally, the little giant, he chose his student, which was me. So that evening, Mr. Baby Lawrence, I think he was invited as some kind of celebrity. He had to be a celebrity up in a nightclub, an after hours club that was called Dickie Wells'. So we started to play in this -- see, this game points is -- you have to -- whoever gets the cue ball the closest from one cushion to the other, lengthwise, they wouldn't have to break the balls, see? And so we did that. He said he would break the balls. He was also spiting us there. Well now, Don Redmond was an expert. He was really a champion pool player, you know. He shot billiards. And he could make the cue ball actually talk, you see. And he could play one ball and he's in position to play the next ball and so forth and so on. Now, it was up to he and

I to make 475 points. So what happened is Mr. Bill Bojangles Robinson, he broke the balls and it was very safe. There didn't seem like there was any way of making a ball, pocketing a ball, you see. But, as I say, Mr. Don Redmond, he was a teacher, see, and very expert in this art. So he saw a ball he could pocket, and also opened a ball where he would get the other balls closer to the pocket, see? So that's what he done. And he started to shooting, he run up to 444 balls before he would miss. When he would miss a ball, he would leave Bill Bojangles Robinson kind of what they call hid. He couldn't find a shot, you see. So he'd have to expose the cue ball or play safe, see? And in order to play safe you have to hit one ball and make one ball go to the cushion. It could either be the ball you hit or the cue ball, you see, as long as you hide the cue ball where the competitor wouldn't have a chance to pocket a ball, see, a point. So the highlight of the game is that you have to bank the last point, see, so somehow it happened there that the play got tighter and tighter, see. I didn't get a chance to run but 19 of the balls, you see, but they was all easy shots, because Mr. Don Redmond had taught me how to do this. You make one ball and make the other balls get closer to the pocket, so you could pocket them. And it was always 15 balls in a rack, and that's what happened. I banked the last ball, you see. And we won. But that was

-- I hadn't seen Mr. Bill Bojangles Robinson till up to that time, see. He was having like his 52nd birthday, I think it was, at the RKO Palace in Boston, and I was wearing a derby at that time. We had become Chuck and Chuckles and so forth. I don't think he knew about that, because we didn't have the Chuck and Chuckles name at the time I met him, see. I was just Shorty, see. But the thing about it, he didn't know where I was from. He didn't know I was from the south or anything, and we got up there and he liked to play that game, you know. He liked to shoot pool. He made a complaint after he saw the show. Chuckles and I went out there and stopped the show. First it was Peg Leg Bates, he went out and he stopped the show. He was the one leg dancing fool. And then they had like Louise McCarroll, she sang, and the band played. Then they introduced Chuck and Chuckles. Chuck and Chuckles stopped the show. They had to do encores. So somehow -- he got indignant about that, you know. So he goes out front to the manager's office, and he says to the theater manager, "Chuck and Chuckles will have to go." So the theater manager said, "Well, now, I'm paying Bill Bojangles Robinson, the world's champion tap dancer, $5,000.00 a week, and I'm paying Chuck and Chuckles $500.00 a week," he said. "If you was to -- if anyone would have to go it would have to be Bill Bojangles Robinson, the world's champion tap dancer," see? So he didn't want to lose his job so he gets out of the manager's office in a hurry and

he come backstage, and he sends his valet over to Chuck and Chuckles' dressing room. And he wants to meet us. He wants to see who we are and what they do and who are they, this, that and the other. So that's what the valet did. He came and told us about Mr. Bojangles was having a birthday cake, getting ready to cut the cake, and he would like for us to come over, Chuck and Chuckles to come over, and have a slice. And wish him a happy birthday. So that's what we did. We went over there, he liked company, see, Bojangles, so he starts to talking and asking questions. "Who's your father," and, "Who's your mother," and, "Who's your uncle," and, "Who's your brother." "Why do you wear the derby?" "What kind of tap dancing is that you're doing?" Now, most tap dancers would say, "I'm tapping like Bill Bojangles Robinson," you know. And if he was satisfied that your tap dancing was good enough to tap dance like him, well, he would smile, you know, and say, "That's good. That's what you should always say." But I told him, I said, "Well, that's because of the office. They insisted that I wear a derby, on account of the Governor of New York State," you know. So he said, "I like you. I like the way you talk. Don't I know you?"
This is Tape Number Twelve of Chuck Green.
Yeah, well, as I was saying, Mr. Bill

Bojangles Robinson, how we became friends. He asked me, he says, "I like you. I like the way you talk. Who are you? Who is your father? Who is your mother? Who is your sister? Who is your brother? Where are you from? Do you play pool?" Said, "Seems like I know you." "What do they call you?" So I told him, "Well, they used to call me Shorty." I said, "I remember you from that night at the gaming room." He laughed and said, "Oh, yeah. You was that pool shooter there's partner. You was with this same man that was leading his orchestra now Don Redmond." I said, "Yeah. Yeah." He said, "You know it's my birthday, my birthday today." He says, "And I'm quite sure I sent my valet to invite you to have a slice of the cake, you know. Well, you're going to have a slice of cake with me, aren't you? Wish me a happy birthday." I said, "Well, I guess so, sure. Sure enough." He says, "Say, look here, do you still shoot pool like you did with that Don Redmond?" And so I explained to Mr. Bojangles that night. I said, "Well, during the time that you challenged us I was just getting ready to take another pool lesson, and that's why he chose me as his partner." So, he laughed again. He said, "Well, you know, I'm not supposed to do anything but happy things during this week. How would you like to go out with me and we'll go and get some ice cream, and we go and go to some pool room and shoot some pool?" Said, "You know, that's my sport. I like that, you know. I'm known as a sport, you

know." So we did. Now, when we gets there, he said, "I'll tell you what. We'll play a," -- he said, "I like the way you tap dance you know. I was looking for you to do some of my tap dance, but I noticed I didn't see any," he said. "But I like the way you tap dance." He said, "I'll tell you, we'll play pool, say, whatever ball that we pocket, that's how many tap steps you'd have to do." So I said, "Yes, sir. Well, what are we going to call the game?" And he said, "We'll call it New America." So I did. I loved his tap dancing, so I was hoping I could get him to do -- make the highest number of balls, you see. He'd have to do that many tap steps. He didn't notice at first, but eventually he caught on. He said, "What are you, trying to learn yourself some of my tap dancing?" He said, "Well, look here, I want to teach you some of my tap steps. I think I know your favorites." And that's how I learned how to do that 32 bars of tap steps, you see, that I demonstrated earlier for you. We became great friends. He wants to adopt me. He wants me to be like his nephew. And I'm supposed to call him Uncle Bill. He said, "Wouldn't you like to call me Uncle Bill?" And I said, "Well, I can't call you Uncle Bill. I've already got an uncle." And he said, "Yeah? What's his name?" I said, "John W. Bubbles." "Oh, Buck and Bubbles. That's right. That's where you all, Slim and Shorty, came from Buck and Bubbles." He laughed again. He said, "All right. We won't fall out over that." And we

remained friends, but as I said, the show was only playing there, he was only appearing a week, he was there with us. He was on a personal appearance tour, so we done that week together. Like to have got held over, you see, but the show had to move on. Happy go lucky from there.
(Recording interruption)

Eventually, Chuck and Chuckles went on further, and we were on another tour. What they call, we was out of our apprenticeship then. We was going on to become stars, which a lot of the show folks were in hopes of happening, because we were getting to be young men then.
This was about what age?
Well, I suppose I was about -- that was 1942, I'm quite sure.
So you were getting famous in a certain way at that time?
Yes, sir.
Were you making a lot of money?
Yes. We were up to $500.00 a week.
Was that apiece?

No. No. No. It was just between the two of us. It was an agreement we had with the office, you know. We probably got more money, but a certain amount of the monies was being sent to our families by Nat Nazarrax, see, because he was still managing us, you see. And the Chuck and Chuckles.
Was Lucille O'Shea taking any percentage of your money at this point?

Yeah. Well, it was the original contract. The contract was for life, see. That's why I say that we were probably making more money, but some of the money was going towards the contract and our families.
So how much money would you end up pocketing?
Well, myself, I would have approximately maybe $650.00 apiece we were getting at that time.
And how much would you get, yourself, alone, after the money had been given to your parents, to your mother and --

Well, I would always get the $250.00, you see. That was sufficient for me, because it was kind of -- the work was kind of steady, because as I say, Chuck and Chuckles was on the increase, from stopping so many shows, you see, and we became the Kennedy favorites, right after that, about a year and a half or so after that, and by the way, in the same city, Boston, Massachusetts. And we had played the Boston Conservatory of Music so many times, and that's why we were going into stardom, because there was an important height in show business at that time. Anyone who had played the Boston Conservatory of Music was considered, you know, a principal act.
But at this time were you performing alone or were you still with Buck and Bubbles?
No, we were with Chuck and Chuckles at this time.
So when did the Buck and Bubbles era end?
Well, that ended in 1936, I think. 1934. I beg your pardon.
Was there any particular reason why it ended?

Yeah, well, Mr. Bubbles, he got pneumonia, and then he recovered, but he had had a wisdom tooth out, and about a week later he contracted double pneumonia, you see, and he had a bout with it again. So he recovered that bout, see, and while he was sick he allowed us to appear in Connie's Inn, places like that, and live away from the apartment, his family and so forth.
Did you move into a place by yourselves?

Yes. We moved into the Woodside Hotel, and then from the Woodside Hotel we went to the Shore Hotel, and we went back down to the Belvedere Hotel. Then we went over to Mr. Nat Nazarra's new apartment and --
Was this the height of your career at this point?
Yes. We had -- look, we went to about --
the Bill Bojangles -- after the Kennedy Favorites -- we became the Favorites, that's when the height of our career really progressed.
And you were getting paid the most at this particular time that you had ever been paid.
Yes.
And you were ever to be paid.
Yes.
That was about $600.00 a week.
Uh-huh.
Apiece. That's what we got.
650 a week apiece.
It was about $1,300.00 that the Chuck and Chuckles act got.
You were being treated fairly, I would imagine, with the money?
Yes, we were. Uh-huh.
Were there any mis-communications or mis-happenings with the money, or producers, at that time?

No, no. There was always an increase. We always would get increases in pay. That's another way, they knew that the money was going -- we were getting popular. More in demand, as they said in show business.
And what was happening to other tap
dancers? Was Hollywood at a boom at that point?

Yeah. The whole country had to get on their toes, you know. To keep from thinking about the Depression. They was supposed to overcome the Depression. Like the series they've been having here recently, where the city went into some kind of budget disruption or something. Well, the Depression was similar.
But you were doing all right during the Depression.

Yeah, we were, because of -- that was one of the main things about the country at that time, was theaters, entertainment. That was a good outlet for people, to overcome their worries, see, financial responsibilities, I should say.
So Chuck and Chuckles now are on their own. What did your -- what were some of the things that you used to do, now, at this particular time, as an act?

Well, we introduced new songs and new tap dances and so on. And Chuckles eventually learned how to play a musical instrument, which was the vibraphone. And we had become honorary musicians by being with Buck and Bubbles. They made us members of the musicians' union. And most of the unions at that time.
He played the vibraphone. He didn't tap dance?
Yes.
On the vibraphone?
No, no. He played them.
Because I know there are tap dancers that do that.

Yes, there was one -- well, there was originally two. I mean, the vibraphone. Will Mahoney danced on the xylophone or the marimba, and then there was a newcomer, Jimmy Smith, he's the one that danced on the vibraphone. But he made this, you know, by hand. He made the instrument himself.
So tell me some of the -- can you tell me some of the routines that you used to do, some of the joking you used to do, and maybe even some of the dancing at this point?

Yeah, well, it mostly consisted of introducing new songs, like, 'Scatting at the Kit Kat,' 'Born to Swing,' and 'Kangaroo,' that was the new dance, but it was mostly visual. There was an off-Broadway show, we introduced that song about the kangaroo, and Chuckles invented, created, a step. It was just one step. It wasn't a whole dance.
What was the step called?
The Kangaroo.
It was a tap step?
Yeah. It was.
Can you do that?
Well, it's only eight bars of music, you see.
I think I'd like to see that one, too.
It's something similar to the Tacky Annie, but you do it I think about four times instead of once, on each side of the body.
Shall we try it?
Sure. I'll give you a degree.
Here we go.
Here we go. The Kangaroo.
(Mr. Green tap dancing.)
That's the Kangaroo. Eight bars.
That is a bit like the Tacky Annie, but not quite as sophisticated.
Can you do the Tacky Annie?
Yes.
(Mr. Green tap dancing.)
That's the Tacky Annie.

That's the Tacky Annie, yes. That was the Tacky Annie. The Tacky Annie, of course, you use both feet equally, and I see with the Kangaroo you were doing something more on one foot more than the other. Would you agree with that?
Yes.

As I say, it's not as sophisticated as the Tacky Annie. The Tacky Annie is really a nice dance step. It looks lovely on girls, I think. It's really a lovely step for girls. I was about an animal, the Kangaroo, and it's that hopping.

(Inaudible). Chuckles, he invented the step. They seemed to like it, you know. We would never do any tap dance routines unless it was agreed for to do by the office, Nat Nazzarro, or Bubbles, either one, you see. At that time, see. But that was in a show for Mr. White, you know, George White, the George White Scandals. Well, he introduced this other show he called -- I think it was the New Shuffle Along of 1930 -- something -- '37 or '8, somewhere in there.
It was about 30 something, -- Shuffle Along.

Yes. The New Shuffle Along was based on some visitors to Africa, and they was deep in the jungles and they had costumes made up of different animals, these visitors. They would have these costumes made like they was some other animal, in case they -- to avoid danger, see. But the thing about it is Africa wasn't Australia, and that's where the Kangaroo was. But it was mostly -- it was about comedy. It was happy times, you know. It was during the Depression, and they was getting over the Depression at that time, and --
Well, what was happening on Broadway
then, as far as tap dance was concerned?

Well, most of the theaters were busy. They were all lit up. They had big shows, hit shows. Even the Ziegfeld Follies was in the profession at that time. He was discovering these new beauties of stage, you know, and so forth, and the Copacabana. Well, all the theaters, they were all lit up, you see, and they was flourishing, you see. Everything was -- Shubert's Alley, all the theaters were going, all up and down Broadway, and they called it the Great White Way, and all of this, you know.
Well, what happened to Chuck and Chuckles? Why didn't they go to Broadway?

They did go. They were up and down Broadway. Chuck and Chuckles was -- well, they doubled on Broadway. They were playing the Capitol Theater and the Roxy Theater at the same time. They were doubling, you see. As I say, Chuck and Chuckles was finally getting to be like next to Buck and Bubbles as a comedy team, because we had become young men then, see. And so we was in -- all in the Depression, right on through the Depression right on into the so-called good days. Happy days are here again, you know. They used to feature that melody a lot, you see.
But Chuck and Chuckles never performed in any Sissle and Blake musicals, did they?
Yes. Well, that was part of it, you
see, because the new Shuffle Along was -- he featured them in that. Noble Sissle and Blake was in the new Shuffle Along and Buck and Bubbles also, see?
But Chuck and Chuckles wasn't.

Well, yes, you could say that. They were Chuck and Chuckles. We worked together, and when we became Chuck and Chuckles, our paths crossed, and that was one of the times. Our paths crossed, where we were on the same bill as Buck and Bubbles. But we were like a separate act at that time. We weren't just in their act. And that was Shuffle Along, you had a script. You had to play parts.

Well, I'd like to get into a little bit of what Chuck and Chuckles' routines were, in terms of comedy, what kind of comedy they did, and if you can recall any of those routines, like you did with Buck and Bubbles before.

Yes. Well, the Chuck and Chuckles routines consisted of the same format, telling of the jokes. Like they'd do a song and a dance and they would exit. And then one of them, which was Chuck, myself, would run back on stage until Chuckles would call him and stop him. And he would say these jokes about, 'What you running for? Looks like it's going to rain out there. I don't want to get wet. See, I've got on a rented costume.' 'It ain't you're scared of getting wet. You're afraid of lightning.' I'd say, 'Who's afraid of

lightning?" He'd say, "You are." "The other day a thunder-storm came up, the lightning flashed, and you ran down into the dark cellar and hid." I'd say, "Well, I've got to protect myself." And he'd say, "Well, protect yourself? Don't you know if lightning's going to hit you it's going to hit you?" And I'd say, "Well, if lightning's going to hit me, leave it look for me."
That's the same as with Buck and Bubbles.
Yeah.
Did you continue that act? In other words, you continued that from the Buck and Bubbles routine and did it as a solo?

Well, the jokes we did. We continued doing the jokes. And we added like new jokes to the continuity, like say for instance, I said Chuckles began playing the vibraphone, you see? So somewhere along in there he would walk out of the spotlight and go and bring on the instrument, vibraphone. So when I look around and see him pushing it out of the wings onto the stage, and I'd ask him, I'd say, "Say, Chuckles, what's this you've got there?" He'd say, "These is vibraphones. I made them." I'd say, "You made them?" He'd say, "Sure I did. I walked into the music store and the man wasn't looking, so I made them." And then I'd ask him, I'd say, "Well, now, Chuckles, can you play them?" He'd say, "Can

I play them?" "Did you ever hear of Lionel Hampton?" And I'd say, "Sure, I did." Then I'd say, "What's his name?" He'd say, "Who?" And I'd say, "Lionel Hampton," and he said, "Never heard of him." And then he began to play, "Lady Be Good".
Did you dance to it when he played?

Yeah. But it was -- what a dance. It was just a short little ditty, you know. It was a fast, up-tempo dance, just to sell his instrument, his playing of the instrument, you see. And I only did like 32 bars of tap dancing, you see, and that was that. Then we had some old jokes, we told some old jokes about, "What was you doing with that old black goat I seen you with?" I'd say, "Well, my black goat can give white milk," and he said, "Well, that ain't nothing." And I'd say, "Well, can you give it?" Or, he asked me, he says, "I do a little tap dancing," and I'd stop, and he says, "That was good." I'd say, "I know it." He'd say, "Chuck, did your father and mother give you money to learn how to tap dance like that?" I'd say, "They sure did." He said, "Well, what did you do with the money?" Then we'd get into a little fight, and he'd shove me away and I'd run at him, and he'd throw up his foot, you see. He's got the advantage in the fight. So he'd say, "Keep it up, so I can reincarnate you." And I said -- and I laughed. And he said, "What you laughing for?" I said, "There you go, talking about reincarnation, and

you don't even know what kind of flower that is." And he laughs, and I say, "What you laughing for?" He said, "Reincarnation ain't no flower. That means when you die you comes back in the form of some kind of animal." So I said, "Is that what that is?" He says, "Sure." And I'd say, "Sure is." And that gets a laugh. And I asked him, "Well, Chuckles, when you die and come back, what kind of animal are you going to be?" He said, "Well," and he looks me up and down, "I think I'll come back in the form of a baboon so I can get even with you." So then I laugh, and he said, "Man, what are you laughing for?" I said, "Man, you can't come back into the same thing twice." Then the band would strike up some music and we'd do a tap dance and exit.
That's a funny routine. That's a funny routine. So what kind of dancing would you exit with?
Well, we would exit with a chase. We'd be chasing each other, see. It would take two people to do that. It was a chase tap dance, see.
A chase tap dance.
Yeah. He'd be chasing me and I'd wind up circling him and chasing him off, like that.
So what was it like on Broadway at that time?
Well, it was milk and honey at that time. Especially for show business, because they began to move the

nightclub shows into theaters also. And that was because it was better increases in pay. Everyone's finances began to improve. And they kept it up until -- right up until the early '40s, see, and they went out with the battle of bands. That's how it went out, began to let up, you know. When they didn't have so many shows, wasn't so active.
Would you say it was milk and honey for the black performer or for all performers?
Yeah.
Was black in at that time?

Yeah. Well, that's why I said it was particularly for the blacks. See, the blacks wasn't as plentiful as the whites. But I mean, just to be appearing in an interracial show, like -- (recording interruption) So it was particularly an advantage and a great improvement for the blacks because they began to work also in the theaters from nightclubs, and then it went on up to around in the early -- till the battle of bands, and Benny Goodman became King of Swing, went into that, went out with the battle of bands, but they still continued variety shows.
But you were performing primarily in New York City at that time.
Yeah. Well, a lot in New York City and then around New York City. We went from coast to coast at least four times, see. We went on tours with Louis Armstrong's

band, and that's when he acquired the Louis Russell Orchestra. That's right after W.C. Handy went with Louis Armstrong's band, and the Louis Russell Orchestra, went out to Los Angeles, and back down to New Orleans. That was during the Mardi Gras and so forth, and he was at great fame then. He was practically the most famous jazz musician we had during those years. He was always a great recording star, you see, Louis Satchmo Armstrong, and we got to be like regular families, you see. But as I say, Chuck and Chuckles were very fortunate, because they were -- they came through apprenticeships and was always a hit, and continued success followed them.
I'm curious to know what it was like with Louis Armstrong, what sort of fellow he was, what kind of stuff you did with him.

Well, he liked our dancing. He liked our act, you know. And he was another great spirit of people, I mean. He was always -- he caused a lot of happiness wherever he was at, see, because he was a personality, as they called them in them days, those years, and they didn't say character so much. They would say personality.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

This is tape number 13 of Chuck Green. Tape number 13 of Chuck Green. So, you were talking about Satchmo and performing with him.
Yes.
He was a unique character.
Yes, he was a great personality.
And I understand you got very close to him.
Yes, got so close he started to calling me son.
Well, I'm very interested in the kind of relationship you formed, and how he responded to tap dancers and how he incorporated that in his own act.

Well, he insisted on us doing a dance. He liked to see me dance like John Bubbles at that time, because John Bubbles was known as a great jazz singer. And he liked to see me dance -- tap dance -- 'Lady Be Good', you see. As I say, it was more like a band leader dancing, you see. It was something in the dance that he enjoyed. I guess it was the circling, I think it was. It reminded him of his trumpet, you see.
Well, what kind of dancing did you do with him? Can you explain some of it -- and I'd also like to see it.

Well, I call it syncopated tap, you see, and of course it was up tempo, very fast, you know. It was a jolly, a merry tempo in tap dancing, you see. Chuckles would be playing his solo on the vibraphones and Chuckles has acquired a new style of comedy. He would operatic singing -- scat singing but he would do it operatically, you see, like some opera star, you know. And he was actually singing operatic, but he'd be scatting, you see, which I couldn't do (unintelligible) a lot of range, you know. But the tap dancing would happen like right after he'd play the introduction -- he played the introduction -- eight-bar introduction, then he'd go into the melody of "Lady Be Good." So, he would play like a chorus and I would tap dance a chorus and come back around like and lead the band for the next half of a chorus going out. That's what Satchmo enjoyed. In case sometime we would have to do an encore, he would make us repeat this number, "Lady Be Good," so he could see the tap dance again, you see. That's what we did.
Can you show me what it was like?
Well, I can show you the tap step that he liked in the tap dance. Would that be all right?
That's fine.
(Recording interruption)
(dancing and humming)
(Recording interruption)
Is there something you'd like to say, Chuck, about the dance you just did?
Yes. Well, it became a favorite of Louis

"Satchmo" Armstrong, and quite a few others, you know, but he was about the most important one to recognize the difference in the tap dancing, you see, because I was always trying to -- I introduced a new degree into tap dancing from the fraternity and John Bubbles' teachings, you see. Mr. Peg Leg Bates -- he taught me a step that was a favorite of mine and I asked him was I doing it correctly? And evidently he liked to see me do the dance step, see. It was from the One Leg Dancing Fool, you see. He would make me repeat the step over and over and over again, you know, then he -- finally he would say, "Yes, you did it better," he'd shout, "Next time I see you, I want to see you do it the way it should be did," you know. So, that's how we became friends.
(Recording interruption)
Well, what do you feel the tap dancing did to the music? What did it bring to the music?

It brought a greater continuity to the improvisation in music, because it was -- it was like a mixture of two jazzes -- one jazz and another jazz. See, they had composed the jazz song called "New Jazz," you see. That's when swing was beginning to go out, you see. This was after -- some time after the battle of bands. George White had went back to Europe, as I say, the New Shuffle Along introduced a new singer which became Bess and -- "Porgy and Bess," the American operetta, by George Gershwin. So, --
So, now Chuck, you and Chuckles were

really blooming after all your -- taking all your classes and you developed now fully into a great first-class act, and mostly you headlined with big bands which were also in the vogue at this particular time. Wouldn't you say so?
Yes, that's absolutely what happened.
The arrow was changing, wasn't it? It was moving from one entertainment form to another for tap dancers.
It was going through a transition.
Yes, it was. Yes. Performers were more plentiful and more fully developed, and they were happy with each other. They were happy with the entire profession of show business.
Big bands -- now, this seemed to be the style of the big bands now. A well-known big band usually -- always took a couple of great singers and a great dancing act or a great dancer with them.
Yes.
And, of course, you now were at this -- this was your peak.
Yes.
You were fully developed. You'd left Buck and Bubbles.
Yes. And they -- what they had done, you see, they eventually started to putting the bands up on
stage where before they would generally play in the orchestra pit as they called it.
It's funny, now, at this time it really was beginning to be the dancers with the jazz -- dancers with jazz --
Music.
-- music.
Yes.
This is interesting.
So, now the big bands were becoming the prominent feature of the show.
Yes.
They were on the stage. And the tap dance -- what happend to tap dancing? Didn't the big bands tend to drown out the taps?

Well, they tried to, but they couldn't do this because of the tap dancers themselves -- they was always introducing these degrees, and they would always have their own music especially orchestrated to fit their tap dancing. But they would always have some kind of new jazz arrangements, because it was specially written for tap dancing. Therefore, the musicians had to play a different type of jazz.
So, basically the tap dancers were affecting the type of jazz that was being done.
Yes, but it was improving. It was all for
the best, see. They couldn't do any worse -- they had just come out of the depression.
Well, it made a large, glittery show -- big band on stage.
But how did the music -- the actual music begin to change?
Well, the music changed because of the tap dancers. They would always have their music specially written for them, you see.
No, I mean the type of music.

Well, it didn't change. It became popular. I mean, swing is what was going out and jazz was coming in, see. Jazz was beginnig to be recognized as a happier -- the happiest music they were playing, and the tap dancing going along with it made it more recognizable, see.
This was what period of time?
Well, this was in the early 40's, right after the battle of the bands.
That gave a better visual understanding of the jazz music.
Yes.
Jazz dancers.
Uh-huh.
And the musicians, I would take it, to start picking up on the tap dancers and what they could do?

Yes. They even started to imitate them. The improvisations that the tap dancers did, in their tap dancing. --like say, for instance, They began to realize that it was jazz (Unintelligible) Lester Young -- the late, great Lester Young. He composed a piece called "Let the Good Times Roll" and I was warming up one day on the stage, you know, just tap dancing. Because We had been riding and sitting down, you know, riding -- your muscles has a tendency to retract, you see. So, I was -- called myself getting limber, you see -- warming up. And he happened to come there, and he was a young musician then, a young tenor player -- saxophonist, and eventually became the president of saxophone, tenor saxophone. He said, "I'm going to warm up. I hope I don't disturb you what you're doing -- your tap dancing. Maybe what I'm playing will go along with what you're going to -- well, let's do some measures." So, he happened to play this melody, "Let the Good Times Roll", and it eventually became the theme song to the Symphony Sid's disk jockey program on the radio. So, I acquired another friend. (Laughter).
Did you dance to the music when he played it?
Yes. It fit it. I was doing measures and tap dancing and he was doing measures and jazz music. But his music was actually "Let the Good Times Roll".
So, you were complimenting each other.
Yes.
Musician -- dancer, dancer -- musician.

Yes. It was a way of saying keep going, keep on, you know. See, this was all between shows. This was either before the show, you know, because it'd have to be before the show because the shows was appearing with moving pictures then.
And you were developing more, of course.
Oh Yes, always.
Because when a good musician plays well, it inspires you to make up new steps and try out new things.
Well, what was the tap dancer's relationship with the drummer, for example?

Well, they were what they call blood brothers, because the drummer played the rhythm for the music of the band, and the tap dancer is all rhythm, see. So, it's as simple as that. That's the relation to the drummer, you see. Like, you had the tempo by the drums, you see.
We're into the -- what would you say, the late '30's now?
No, I'd say early '40's, '41, '42, like that.
And who are the -- what other dancers
Well, most of --
-- Besides you and Chuckles?

Well, most of the greats they had -- Roland James of Sonny and Sonny, Sonny Austin of the Four (Unintelligible) and Baby Lawrence of the Harlem Highlanders. Well, then, Groundhog -- he was coming out of retirement at another time -- at that time. Because he had been a popular dancer with the Whitman sisters. And then you had Taps Miller -- that was the tap dancing trumpet player. He composed songs like, 'Wham, rebop, boom, bam, I'm killer-diller, yes I am. Wham, bebop, boom, bam, I can sing and I can jam.' And he would tap dance and he'd play the trumpet, you know. dancers began Tap dance was beginning to like variate you see, they tried to add a little different characters to their routines, you know. George Rochette used to come out with three dishes and he'd turn them upside down and he would tap dance on the three dishes, see. That was known as novelty tap.
Let me ask you, did novelty tap start prior to this particular era, which is the big band era? Were there novelty acts?
Oh, yes, yeah. Will Mahoney was a novelty act by dancing on the marimba, see, and --
I think what we'll do now, rather than go into all the particular dancers, continue with Chuck's
career.
I thought we'd --
And then later we will get back into all the dancers that you met through your career and their particular styles. And also how they influenced you and the change of their styles through the years.
Yes. Well, there were only two that inspired me, and that was J. D. -- which I called "Slim" Chuckles, and John Bubbles of Buck and Bubbles, you see.
All the other dancers you didn't find that --

No -- I -- I enjoyed them immensely, but I'm saying they weren't an influence on me -- well, there was two more, there was Raymond Winfield and Walter Beaty, you know. I had my moments, too, you know. I was -- I would rather do an original work than try to do something -- an impression of another tap dancer, see. It's like introducing a new degree to tap dancing. Eventually you can create -- you can introduce a creation, see. Like eventually be a Bill Bailey -- after Terry Wilson discovered him he went away for about -- about four weeks on his own somewhere, and he came back with a new creation of tap dancing which is -- had the one-foot cramp and all that in it. See, because tap dancing then was almost -- most of them was trying to learn how to do the John Bubbles which is cramps, you know, and the kick cramps and the tap

turn, you see. And he had ways of doing -- performing that was infectious to other people that especially was in the same art -- tap dancing, you know. Well, the fraternity used to call them desserts -- like the end of the meal you have the sweets, you know, and that's the way they used to appear, you know. It was like a refreshment, you know.
So, now, the first big band for you to appear with was who?
The first big band we appeared with was actually Chick Webb.
This was prior to Louis Armstrong or --
Yes.
Uh-huh. Why don't you tell me a little bit about that?

And he hadn't discovered Ella Fitzgerald yet. And we were playing there and we was breaking in a new routine -- a new tap dance, and they used to have tap dancers' night down there on Fridays. They'd have a searching spot light -- a spot light would go searching through the audience and the master of ceremonies, he would be -- already had spoken to the

projectionist -- the light man, electrician, and tell him who's sitting in the audience and where to stop the light. And whoever the light stopped on, they would have to get up and do one chorus of their version of a tap dance they was calling the Shim-Sham Shimmy. It was really from a chorus girl's encore dance. And that's what happened, see. Well, he eventually got -- he overcome -- he overcome the double pneumonia, you see, and -- but we were doing so good then until they decided that we should be an act all of our own, you see. Because the money was better and it would be better if we were out of their act, you know, and doing an act of our own, you see. Like that -- get more money that way.
Talking about the Shim-Sham Shimmy, I'm wondering whether --

That's what it was, you see. But that dance -- it was all right, it really -- sometimes it stopped the shows, you see, because everybody doing it -- their version. They couldn't do it like someone they had seen, they had to do it their own way. They had to originate a way of doing the Shim-Sham Shimmy, you see.
Well, did you have a particular way of doing it yourself?
Oh, yeah, I had a particular way, yes.
That's a natural introduction to your doing it for us.
Invitation.
Well, I'll let you see it.
Okay.
(dancing)
So, this is Chuck Green's version of the Shim Sham Shimmy.
That's right.
That was very nice. (Recording interruption) Tell me a little bit about the Shim Sham Shimmy and how that reflected the personality of tap dancing.

Well, it reflected the personality of tap dancing because the chorus girls finally took an encore. Mr. Teddy Blackman -- he was the choreographer at that time at the Lafayette Theater, and sometimes he would go around into Connie's Carny's Inn and assist Mr. Clarence Robinson Robertson, which was another famous choreographer. He did shows for the Carny's Inn and the Cotton Club also -- mostly in the night clubs like Small's Paradise and sometime he did a lot of work for Ziegfield -- Florenz Ziegfield's choreography. And the Shim-Sham Shimmy -- Connie Mr. Carny Immerman who owned the Carny's Inn -- was named after him -- he got this idea of having a dancer's night and because the Shim Sham-Shimmy became famous, everybody wanted to learn it and mostly the people -- the public. They liked to dance and they liked the steps. It was like an education dance. It was a tap dance, you see, and he got this idea of having a

dancer's night. Like when a celebrity -- a lot of celebrities used to come into Connie's Inn -- and they came to Harlem a lot at that time into these night clubs, and you may see anyone there, you see. You may see Dick Powell, the great singer, (Laughter) and some great band leader or somebody known dancers or whoever, you know. It was the master of ceremonies who made the show more entertaining, you see, because the dancer's night occurred after the first part of the show, like during the intermission, see. Well -- I know he was a thespian, therefore, showman. Which was always therapeutic -- and there was -- conveyed more than just dramatics. See? They became jazzists, you see? And, some of them were the true identities of this jazz.
He was a natural, was he?
Yes, he was a natural theater -- theatrical property.
Tell me more, Chuck.

Well, now he had to get into -- he had to let his relations know -- theatrical folks, you know, show folks, he had to let them know that he was like doing some other properties, you know, for the industry, see. And the house -- they have an actors, you know, they got a -- they got places to bless, you see, cause God to degreed in, you
see and --
So he had a very unique talent?
Yeah.
He had a unique style? And you wanted -- he -- you -- you're saying that he was trying to sell that as a commodity, sell it to the agents?

Yes, he was improving management, you see, while you could say manage, he was improving this and he was letting the foundations know. See? That he had some other complexions, I will say, you could say image, see?
Chuck, could you tell us something about these great stories we heard on the grapevine about what the battle of the taps between Teddy Hale and Baby Lawrence?

Yeah, you see the tap dancer's dream, which was Baby Lawrence and he was discovered by the jazz giant, (unintelligible), Don Redman, Teddy Hale, was really the juvenile of the two, because he was -- he hand't been tap dancing as long as tap dancer's dream. Who I like to call Bravery, initially known as Baby Lawrence, now he was dubbed Baby Lawrence by the show folk during the early nightlife up there, I think it was like the Rhythm Club and that -- that new nightclub they had there, they just opened up Morains, you see? And they had the run of the mill in variety, because there was three types of jazz music going on, see? There was this swing,

was being introduced. And -- but it hadn't got popular, you see? Now as I was saying, Teddy Hale was a personage. See, of a shadow, because he played that role. But he was so happy to learn to make his feet, you know, like tap dance. And they used to go around and like musicians, like they'd have their mouthpiece, you know, and they would get on the stand, the band stand and have a -- what they call sit-in, you see? Well the tap dancers, they figured they could do that too, you see. (Recording interruption) Lot of them. They really was after some kind of theme song, you see?

They wanted to keep the composers active, you know, inspired, you know, inspiring and the writers. And, they would get up and have these tap dance tournaments and they would yell out different musical laws, you see. And then they'd say, you know, there is no taps in the picken, but they sure do tap dance the Charleston, you know, there's Charleston tap, there's the Lindy Hop tap, you know. And let's find out who wants some more tournaments.

And -- they would ask the -- some of the musicians say, look, do you know so-and-so-and-so -- they was trying to keep some song popular, like 'If I Could Be With You, Just One Hour' -- you know. See, keep the people patronizing. You see? In other words, they'd make some kind of announcement about their next appearances, you know, wherever, whatever state or you know.
You were talking before about the different type of music that was going on at the same time. Can you tell me a little bit more about that and how it affected the tap dancers?

Yeah, well they was really trying to save the blues, you see, the blues was getting unpopular. See, because they wanted to kind of reject the blues, because the tempo of the blues, they hadn't quite came to the applying tempo, like a beat, see -- blues was more like a ballad. See? On some say it's kind of meditative. Blues. You see, until like Pop -- Ruff Ellington's brother, I mean he -- he did East St. Louis Toodle-oo. And that gave the blues a beat, you see. Someway up here in Columbus Circle there, I think he and Sonny Greer and -- I think Harry Carnegie and Johnny Hodges, you know, and Cootie Williams, Tricky Sam, you know, they was all -- I called them doctors of music because they were so overwhelming, you see. And, there's no way for you not to catch a feeling, I mean, when they'd start like that. I think he retitled that Sitting and Rocking, I think he retitled East St. Louise Toodle-oo. And he was cited by the composer, which was another pop, W. C. Handy. So, this guy, he became very popular, think it was named Rayburn, something -- Ross Rayburn, something like that. He had a -- he had a jazz band, you know, but they played like house music, what they called house music and they would intro-

duce these new works by the composers from ASCAP's, you see, and the off-Broadway shows, like this thing, what was it? It was some (unintelligible) -- think they turned that out too, LEW Leslie and his partner, there. He had a partner, you see? And -- that was the darn -- name of the darned show, I think it was Zanzibar, something. It was called. And, which after those times, I mean, they was going to rename these clubs.

You see the Cotton Club people were going to reinstate themselves, you know, relocated, like they was gonna come down like right on Broadway, right into the -- right into the detail, the degree of it all, you see? And --
In other words, places like the Cotton Club, the Elks Rendezvous -- the Savoy Ballroom, were closing down, is that correct? And they want to sort of popularize tap dance now, back on Broadway?

Yeah, well tap dance never did get unpopular. You see, it just got anaemic, see? The people took their taps off, you see? And that was just -- I guess you would say like some bird leave a nest in a tree somewhere and then they never know when the tree will have that bird again, in the nest, you see, and that -- had to be something else by the time the flock gets back.
Why did they take the taps off the shoes?
Huh?
: Why was -- any particular reason? You say they took the taps off the shoes?

Yes, quite a number of them did, because they didn't have enough choreography -- that's really waht it was. See? They had a-- like what we would call a professor of music, physicist is to science, you see -- even playwrights, they were unknowns -- you see? And people wanted to -- they wanted to get in musicals, you see, and in the musicals they didn't feature a lot of tap dancing. See? It was mostly being visual.

See, like -- like I say, to get -- to get into play like table tennis is today, like you have to volley for the serve. You see? What I mean, they had this versatility, which is tap dancing, you see? In case they was asked, you know, costume departments, and so forth, they would -- they would always outfit the performers, see?

So what was happening with the kind of tap dancing that was going on at this particular time? What was Baby Lawrence and Teddy Hale -- what kind of tap dancing were they doing in relationship to the music? How were they changing tap dancing or was it just the same as it always had been?
No, it wasn't the same as it always had been. Because they kept introducing new works, you see? They reinstating, you see, they'd reinstate it, once they -- like

what they call repertoire. Or medley, see a medley is more than -- it's at least about three or four different songs. And they're melodies, you see? So, the tap dancer's dream, like Baby Lawrence, especially, they just -- Teddy Hale, see now he -- like the bolero, see that was introduced into the jazz media. By this -- this Eddie Haywood's son, Hayward's song, I think. You see. Eddie Haywood, Jr., he did this -- he gave some kind of beat to the Bolero -- which appealed to Teddy Hale, personage, you know, you see.

But he didn't always do his tap dance to that. He was like what you call self-taught. You know, like once they acquire the ability a person has a tendency to use different motives for emotions, you know. It's -- I think it's romancing the art itself, see. Which he was great at, you see, now I'm his teacher, you see, but I just taught him, cause he asked me to, you see? I could understand that, see? But I wasn't allowed to adopt anyone at the time, see, I was under special contract and I was only allowed to do certain things, I had to follow orders. Understand?
Whose orders were you following then?
That was John Bubbles, Buck and Bubbles.
Were you under contract with -- who was Teddy Hale under contract with?
Well I really didn't -- I never found that out, I mean he was originally under contract with Ted Lewis,
you see? The "Me and My Shadow", maestro, bandleader. See?
And what sort of restrictions was John Bubbles placing on you, at the time?

Well that I couldn't -- I wasn't allowed to go back and be a celebrity at all times. I had to be, you know, couldn't be -- have to be careful with exposing one's career. You understand? Like, if you're -- if you're appearing in a place and someone know that you are popular, or it gets -- the word gets backstage they will -- show folk had a tendency to -- you'd either have to get up and take a bow, and sometime the audiences, you know, it'd be fan clubs in them audiences, you see? And they would insist that you get up, if the audience don't do it, the master of ceremonies or whoever they are, you know, would insist on it, maybe the manager or the owner of the -- I mean the place, that's -- you get lectured, you know, by your elders.
So Bubbles told you what in confidence?

Don't -- in other -- other words, not to have too much hero worship. That's what he told me. See? But I was actually trying to help my partner, you understand, my childhood friend, which was -- I call him -- say he was south's favorite son, see as a child, understand? And he was known as Slim -- J. D., you know, he had a couple of names and the public called him this. And he had got a chance to expose being a professional because once -- once upon a time, there,

this -- the master of ceremonies of one of the shows -- he's about now, I think he's been helping me, what'd they call it, something about light -- the blind, you know, they called it something about the light -- the oh, it's some kind of organization of light, you know, about the blind, his name is Johnny Jazz Cousins. Well now his home state was Tennessee, rather his mother, you see, and he was master of ceremony -- a show at one of Tom Bailey's houses.

I think it was the A one. And that's where J.D. was popular, you see, in this city, Atlanta, Georgia. See? And -- he was -- he was building -- he was getting what we call first, you know, like an athlete continues to -- may have set a record, then he'll break the record, then he'll set another record, you know, like this. Now -- why he was a child, then, but I said somewhere earlier, in this -- recording that after Chuckles -- after -- after he got up here, after we got up into this part of the country, above the Mason-Dixon Line, see -- he was a -- he was giving himself other thoughts, other ideas, you know?

Why I was trying to learn or get Mr. Bubbles to teach me how to -- this tap dance, this new tap dance, he was creating, which was rhythm tap dancing, you see? He was -- I say he was fathering it, because he was so expert at it. You understand, he was -- it was like enlarging respiration, I would say that's the way he was to me -- other times, I mean

he would ask me questions, you know, and say things, what're you thinking about today? What's it all about, like that, you know? Being -- he's being a family head, he's like a family man, you see. And I would have to explain. You know, so I would say, Mr. Bubbles, you know I asked Mr. Buck about my -- my partner and how he could change his tap dancing, how he would be able to learn himself how to tap dance like you, at least a few of the steps, you know, because I mean the office is going to be insistent on us being little Buck and Bubbles, eventually, you know.

Say, he say, well, -- he decided right there that day, he said, well I tell you what, he said I'm going to pretend that I'll teach you more than I'm teaching him. Maybe that'll inspire -- that'll reawaken his anxieties, you know? See. I'm -- look here, I'm -- see -- I had a tendency to over -- you know, I would over like someone. I really would, you know, I didn't like to get caught at it, but I was. I had a great inquisitive nature or something, you see, I was always inquisitive, inquisitive, inquisitive -- asking questions, you know.

I used to get a lot of spankings from doing that, see? Until my father used to -- he put a stop to the spankings by having me to go to one of the brothers of the family, which was the Uncle (unintelligible) husband, you know, and I'd have to get a lecture, while I'm going -- you see?
(Recording interruption)

Well now you see, eventually we worked it all out. See? And -- it worked out like Mr. Bubbles said. See? And Chuckles did learn a few of them, you know, but naturally he won't change his style, see? He didn't change his style because it's not easy, you know, it's a way of being versatile, you see and being able to be like what an impressionist is in voice, it can also happen in dance.

He wind up getting the water on the knee, you know? You know, cause that kind of tap dancing, you know, -- you know. But I like to bring this back to the tap dancer's dream and the shadow's personage, which was Teddy Hale, Baby Lawrence and Teddy Hale. And this place, where they used to meet -- was a regular, was called Minton's Playhouse, opened up there in Harlem there, and they was trying to keep their thing down, you know Harlem's Harlem, you understand?

It was a happy community, it always had been and people were very colorful, you know, and they always had been been -- because they would come down just to get something going, say, you know after they leave. But by them being there they'd get a chance to go and frequent places like Minton's Playhouse and that's where they would see all these great happenings. You see?
Now when they say Baby Lawrence and Teddy Hale, they was getting ready -- they was getting ready to do some tournament, that's a tap dancing -- that's a type of tap

dancing, that one has a great freedom, you candegree as much as possible. In other words you can enlarge a study. You know, if you're like some kind of mastermind, you see, a genius is occurring, you see? If you let this genius avoid you, you know, if you're not in control of it at the time, you know, you can't bring off your composition. You see? And that's what they did.

But by them doing this, their appearance is better than the whole show, whatever show they had there, but they didn't have -- they didn't feature no show in Minton's Playhouse, they only had like musicians, you see? Or like singers. Something, you know. It was like what they call showcasing today. They called it, showcasing. See? And it's really was a dedication to this one maestro, Teddy Hill, he had orchestra, you know, and he gave up his orchestra, just to manage this place, you see? And he was like the master of ceremonies, you see?

But once the ball started to rolling, you know, they -- they -- there it was, see? Cause they come in, they kept coming and going, you never know when they leaving, you know when they coming and going, you know, if you know when they're leaving, it's because sometimes, I mean, people had to socialize with them, you see and they'd have to go out like that, you see.
Well, how did the audiences respond to them?

Oh, my goodness, whew. You could -- you could hardly hear your ears, I mean when they finished something, because it was new, you see and see they educate the public, because the public at that time, they wanted to learn -- like if they see something that they'd like to have something -- I think it -- I can do that, and sitting in the audience. You know how one analyzes? You know? They would have to explain it when they left, someone asked them, where you been what did you do and so forth, they would have to explain what they did or what they saw, or something, it was interesting, you know, did you have a nice night, and so forth.
Well what was so different about their way of tapping? That hadn't -- the public hadn't seen?
It was one of a kind -- it was like an instrument. Like a trombone is not a trumpet. Like that.
In other words, what you're saying at this point in time, tap dancing had transcended the dance form and had become --

No, John I'm not saying tap dancing, I'm not saying the art, I'm saying these personalities, Baby Lawrence and Teddy Hale -- they were one of a kind -- they didn't -- they wasn't like because they're tap dancers and that's a tap dancing -- that -- they're not in unison. See, they're different personalities of the art.
And they -- basically transcended
the dance form and made it an instrument within the band, rather than a dancer with a band, they were an instrument in the band.

They were a musical -- there was music. They were music, themselves. See, cause tap dancing is a material, you know like -- like they do -- they call it a capella -- that's what I -- that's without musical accompaniment, you see, accompaniments, you see? That's -- you just hear the tap dancers, you know, the tap and the -- and the floor, you see, that's what that is.

Now a lot of times audiences used to come in a place and Baby Lawrence and Teddy Hale would already be there. And they'd be up on the floor and there nobody playing a musical instrument. But you would hear them and a lot a -- of times, like the projectionist, you know, has got to come down, like turn the lights on -- so forth, you understand? But it was -- like say for instance you go to a great playground or recreation place, you know, and you -- you know, -- you never know, you may see like a Harlem Globetrotter out there somewhere playing at one of these places -- they teach -- you know, self-preservation, you see.
But I'm just saying, that audiences some of them were fortunate you know, say I remember when, they could say this --

Can you demonstrate, Chuck, for us some of the kind of tap dancing that these artists did?

Yes. Yes. Say, for instance now, Teddy Hale tapped danced, and I started off like he did, you know. It's the way I taught Teddy (inaudible). I mean, You have to ask yourself the compromises. Okay. I'll compromise (inaudible). (Mr. Green demonstrates some tap dancing steps.)

one that could do that, I see, besides myself. But I never do what -- like if I learned a student anything, it's theirs, you see. It's just like bucking a private, you see.

Well, Baby Davy (unintelligible) the same you see.

that's Baby Davy Lawrence, see. It's partly. See, it hasn't stopped yet. See, that's his part of it. Then he would go into these things.
