That's another part. And he went into patterns. He did this here. He did --
(Mr. Green dances)
Baby Davy Lawrence. And there's quite a lot of them, see. Here's another one he did.
(Mr. Green dances)
See, like that. That's Baby Lawrence.
Certainly is.
(Mr. Green dances)
See, that's the break he had.

Yeah. Well, his style -- yeah, I could show you more parts. He did this here.
(Mr. Green dances)
See, that's an hors d'oeuvre.
It seems to have the Baby Lawrence trademark, I can see, because I've seen him dance and I see it there. Very difficult to do.

So, like they used to demonstrate these tournaments. They acquired themselves a better -- a greater brotherly love, I would call it. And they was always hoping that someday maneuvers would arrive and gather them all together in some kind of mania. And fortunately, it happened to happen to me, you see. And I was talking about -- thinking about how could I do -- what would I do without Chuckles, you see, because Chuckles was -- he was back in the business. But he had got in the situation that I was in in the hospital, you know. He had to pinch hit, you see.

So, he took some fellow's place named Mosley. He used to be in the Three Chocolate-teers. And, well, he got rediscovered. Some woman imported a fraulein over in the fatherland, father-land, and they called her Gesler Gunther, you know. And she happened to see him, or some of her managers or somebody saw the Chocolate-teers over there with -- I think it was something about the Joy Train or something. Duke Ellington, you know.

And she liked the way he was -- his impressions, you know. He was so impressive, you see, because he's tall and he really was what they call -- I call a true slim, you know, because I mean he's -- I couldn't blame the lady, you know. She's fortunate, you see. You see, I thought I was lucky enough to have a friend like that as a child, you see, and to grow up with. But, I mean, you know so much for -- but he became like Jimmy Chuckles Walker, see. He got a chance to use his whole family name, you see.

Well, anyhow, I mean he started to be like some kind of producer. They made him a mascot of her office, I think. That's what I hear. They got some kind of portrait -- picture in the office of him as some kind of mascot.
You lost touch with Chuckles?
Yeah. Well, I didn't loose touch, you know. I found out where he was. We wrote. We communicated, you know, but I was supposed -- on the way to a surprise. I was

going to be surprised by -- like the George Wein office, you see. He's some kind of -- in America he's supposed to be some kind of jazz leader, you know. I mean he represents jazz, like the jazz festivals, you know. Like the Newport Jazz Festivals.
And he had a friend, a great author that used to be a professor in the Mark Hunter College. But he passed on, you know. And --
Who's that?
That's Professor -- it's Jean Stern's husband.
Marshall Sterns?
Yes. Yeah. And so, it's all left on George, see.
Well, what happened? What was Marshall Sterns doing for tap dancers?

Well, what he was going to do, he was going to give them like a world tour, which we call monarchy -- rather I calls it monarchy, when one is fortunate to go around the world and meet all the, you know, the populations, you see. And eventually he was going to make films. He was going to make movies, you know. And he was going to feature like type-cast tap dancing, you see, which I think there's going to be one -- someone, a young film maker like is coming in the future here now -- George C. Nurenberg. He's going to be a

young film maker. I don't know whether he'll bring it over, you know, but he may do it. I guess I'm going to try to help as much as I can about tap dancing as long as I'm in it. I mean that's what Chuckles would have wanted. And when everybody that I know -- my aunt and everybody -- I mean the family, especially John Bubbles, you see. And, you know. And Bill Bojangles Robinson, you know. Because I used to tell stories, Little like traveling experiences, you know.

When you work with somebody great like that, champion, you see, they always have a tendency to give you some -- what I would call a morsel, you see. It's like a food, you know, for one's anxiety, and emotions, and your passions, you know. If you love an artistic motive, you try to treat it as you would a nursery, you see. And that's how you get the value into view where it could be heard; into sound like in the sound systems, you see. And it's for better publication in the libraries throughout the world, you see, because there's going to come a day, you know, when the world's going to sure enough renew itself, you see.

God moves in mysterious ways, you see. See, because I got to -- I had to rejoin the church. And I was already a Baptist, right. So, like not to get off the occasion of the count -- comment is that there's a church up there in Brooklyn in New York City, the Big Apple, you know. Fun Foreign City they calls it now.

And that really is fun, you know, because you can get rebaptized, and also you can get a new (unintelligible) you see. It's called a new cornerstone. And it's a lovely mother woman -- a lady -- she got her son -- grown son (unintelligible). I don't know whether he has made her a grandparent yet. But she was the one that invited me to go and rejoin the church, you know, up there in Brooklyn on Putnam Street.
And I just called the mother Mrs. Rights, you know. And she said, well, you should go, you know. Said God is the one to get your degrees from, you know. So --
Did she have anything to do with you dancing at the Jazz Vespers?
Yes, she did.
With Reverend John Ginzo?
That's right.
Tell me a little bit about that.

Well, she told me to always go to where the parotials (sic) were. Once you get a new doing and rebaptized, you know, that's like -- that's like joining the meeting Christ all over again, you see. And it's really good for anyone. It's like food, you know, to the passions, you see.
Can you tell me a little bit about the Jazz Vespers with Reverend John Ginzo?
Oh, that's new. That's so transparent.
Well, that's the greatest. I think that's the greatest -- what they call it -- I call it -- I say medicine, you know. Because it's a re-awakening of what God is to his own image, you see.
Well, what does Reverend Ginzo do?

Well, he's -- I would say he was in -- he's some kind of -- he's a great author, you see. He's a great authority of anyone's compassion, you know. I mean to the -- you know, the humane personages that's in people's personalities, you see.
What I really mean to say is what has he done for jazz and for tap dancing.

Well, he has -- he's relocated jazz. They should really donate a broadcasting station to this man because -- this reverend, you see, because I think he's the originality of what they call the jazz priest, you see. But only he's a reverend, you see. So, there's a difference in the degrees, see. I think the reverend is kind of a little further on the bone than the priests, you know. He's more like an elder, you see. And like classes, like student bodies, you know, that's -- that wants to remain studious, you know, or they wants to branch out, you know.
(Recording interruption)

You see, he just has -- I think they got a new church now. See, over here, not to get away from the recruiting that I was told to do to reinstate, me. But Mother Mrs. Right, you see. I happened to meet this man -- and I

like to call him "True Student" to myself, you see, because he's a reverend. And my life was saved by a reverend when I was a child, see, because I didn't know nothing about the Swanee River, see. That's how I was baptized. But it was a different body of water. And, like the dark (unintelligible) you see, I wasn't -- I didn't know how to see the light in the dark at that time. But I eventually did.

So, anyway not to speak too much about me as a tap dancer, but I am a kind of an example of what I'm speaking of here about the Reverend -- Jazz Vespers, you see. See, he's John too, you know. He's -- he asked me to come down some Sundays, you know, and this is -- to kind of make his message more open, you know, and to outlet the freedom that the land of the free is all about, you see.

And so, I tries to tap dance for him. I tried to story tap, you see -- I call it because it's like we are supposed to read some kind of passions in the day's lessons each day, you see, especially on the day of rest, see.

I had got reinstated by Oral Roberts, you know. My aunt before she passed -- and she was a WAC. She took me out on Long Island there somewhere, and I had to become -- I got a badge from the revival, see, you know, about Oral Roberts, you see. He gives a person an authority, see, like an officer of religion, you see, an older man or whatever.
But Reverend Ginzo, he -- and the Jazz Vespers -- I

mean he does these summons in the services of God, you see, because he's -- I think he really is a true student, you know, which is -- one never knows, you know, where the roller will begin or end, be (unintelligible) you see. The rolling tide comes in as the tide goes out, right.

But I mean, see, like I tried to get down there on the Sundays, see, because he's liable to be anywhere. You could enlist with the -- if you keep up with these services, your jazz vespers, you see. And it seems to be growing, and I hope that a lot of student bodies will prosper themselves from this, because it's quite a few he has turned out, you know. I'm waiting to read about them. I keeps searching the copies and trying to read about someone that has became popular from the Jazz Vespers, you see.
Who are some of the other jazz musicians that he has at his church?

Well, he has one fellow there that's named Lewis, you know. He's a great pianist, you know. Stanley Turrentine used to play there. There's Matthew Gee. He's continuing to play there. Well, he just had some fellow named John. And John -- I can't think -- I can't remember his last name. But he also plays the piano. He plays several instruments.
Didn't he preside over the Baby Lawrence funeral?
Yes.
